by starbrighter

Summary

Every eighty years, the people of Aedes Elysiae sacrifice a young woman to the ancient being which haunts their forest-bound village. It is the only way to protect everything they hold dear, to keep the shadows that once ate the rest of the world from eating them too.

After centuries of this uneasy peace, it appears the creature's tastes in food have changed.

Now it is Phainon who will be given to the one too terrible to name.

chapters.title: Chapter 1: hespera
chapters.html:
It had always taken girls.

Though it was ten and two years since the last sacrifice, Phainon remembers it clear as the sunset he watches this evening, tied to the great weeping willow and awaiting his fate.

As the sun sinks below the shadowy horizon that encompasses their riverside village, he pictures her as she had been all those years ago. She had seen sixteen summers. Such an age had seemed so grown up, to Phainon. Larger than his own ten and two by far more than four. Dressed in rare white lace with golden clasps, hair braided with water lilies and fern; her favourite family jewellery had hung heavy on her neck as she stood in the late summer breeze.

She had not cried. She had not begged, or pleaded for them to send another, or screamed in terror at the fate that awaited her.

She had met the gaze of every man who lashed her to the bark with unflinching anger. So great was her stare, so terrible and fearless, that Phainon remembers the very hands who tied her trembled as they tightened the last of the knots. No words had been spoken to the last humans she would ever see. The silence had sunk deep into the belly of the earth, and was drunk up by the clear night sky.

But he had felt it, as they all did that night; the silence returning. The silence in the shape of a creature, warped and ancient and wrong as it made the air, seeping beneath the slats of their wooden-woven doors as its terror trod and trampled the earth.

And then, the nothing.

They all remembered the nothing. The strange, absent silence in the shape of a girl stamped on their eyelids as they slept. Though none left their beds in the terror of the everdark night to see, they had not needed to. They all knew the truth as it always had been.

She was gone.

Come morning, the ropes were in a pile amidst the gnarled roots of the weathered tree, severed clean down the middle by some great power a human might ne’re hope to wield. In this it had been done as it had always been done. Eighty years of safety for their village earned through the sacrifice of one; a price those of Aedes Elysiae were always willing to pay.

After all, they were the only place. The only village. The only forest. The only people. There was nothing outside of the shadowy realm that crept about their small paradise; only daemons and deathly spirits, the elders said. Only terrors even greater than the one that kept them safe. Only shades in the shape of men who would lure one to death through their darkness.

Phainon could not remember her name. He had not known it to begin with, young as he had been at the time, and asked all around for anyone who might give it him after she was taken. They told him it was best not to think of her. They told him to pretend she was dead. Phainon had thought even dead people have a name, just like his father, but clearly he would never be told hers no matter how much he begged, and he gave up trying only a few months later.

Yet the peace she gave them was meant to last the entire eighty years. In the rotting books they kept from the damp of the river by carved marble pedestals, laid in a ring around the hearthfire they gathered about each evening to sing and parcel out the dinner the women had hunted from the shadow boundary, the steps for their sacrifice were spelled out in order. First, the creature would make known its hunger needed to be satiated; it would pick at the wild things to begin with, leaving trails of slick blood in place of the traps their hunters had set for game. Then it would turn to the village livestock, tearing from their goats a head and three legs, leaving the bleeding torso twitching and wet for the morning farmers to stumble upon.

This time, however, the village had ignored the signs. Though they had been left wanting for game, though they had discovered in their wooden-stilt pens the body of a sheep and the hoof of a pig, they had pushed this aside with haste.

It had only been ten and two years. It could not yet be wanting for food. This was a fluke, a symptom of the shadows that threatened their borders instead.

The death to draw together a meeting of elders was the loss of their bull. A giant of a creature, larger than Phainon by almost a head, had lay with it black eye open and shining like a bead in its clearing pasture come misty dawn.

A great cut cleaved into the sinewy muscles of its neck; a gash shaped like human teeth, sharpened to a point. The blood was still wet about its fur.

To lose one of only three of their bulls, a mighty animal that could feed and clothe dozens of them for years through its offspring, was a tragedy they would lament for many years. A far greater tragedy than one girl. How many could a girl feed?

Only one.

Only it.

The elders gathered amidst the fire, heads bowed in serious contemplation. Had the creature not liked her? Had it grown tired of her too quickly, as eternal beings might do? Was she not to its liking; was she sick, unsuitable for decades of blood giving?

And so they had tried again. The creature had always taken women, and taken them young, unmarried and with little family who might desire vengeance. Once more they selected the sacrifice – this time a girl of just fifteen summers with no parents or sisters to protest. She was younger, with longer hair and eyes green as the mossy forest floor. She had not been like the one when Phainon was young. She had cried, and begged, and desperately struggled as she was tied to the weeping willow.

And, come morn, she had remained. Asleep at the base of the tree, arms still bound above her head, entirely untouched.

She said she remembered nothing. Only a great darkness, a great shadow, a great hunger so horrifying it made her sob though her cries had made no noise – and then it had disappeared once more.

They had decided its tastes had changed. As with all beings, it sought something new, something to satiate urges humans could hardly comprehend.

They should kill it, Phainon thinks, this thing that haunts their every moment of existence. But how does one take the life of the undying? How does one bring end to a permanence? It was impossible by any standards they could fathom; even more so, for the protection it brought their village from the unknowns of the forest border. What terrors lay beyond the shadows?

No one ever left Aedes Elysiae, and no one ever entered. It was sealed by a great spell of which they could not comprehend, a ward which fended off all manner of terrible creatures and dark matter which threatened to destroy them. They knew this, for it was written; their village was all there is. A single pinprick of existence in a fathomless, formless shadowscape. That was the offering of the violent creature they served. In return for feeding it, for giving it life eternal, those in their village could live in peace, farm and hunt and forage and build. Forever, the wheels of a cart tracking against cobbled stone on a circular path, unending and perfectly content.

Now, Phainon was the offering.

He had not protest when he was selected. What was the opposite of a young maiden, fresh-faced and dew-laden in the twilight? A man, they had decided. Able-bodied, strong. Virile, for perhaps their previous sacrifice has been too weak to withstand the ancient power that wished to feed from her body.

No part of him wanted to be the food of an ancient creature for the rest of his life. No part of him craved whatever lay in wait for him in that dreaded, crumbling castle on the forested hillside outside of their valley. What terrors would he be promised? Perhaps none. Perhaps the creature was true to its name; and simply only wished to drink his blood, and would have him chained and in the dark for the rest of eternity.

“Please– please! Do not have him be taken from me too-!”

From the shuttered bridge stumbles an elderly woman, knobbled knees clacking together with each step.

She makes it no further than the marsh-ground, for those who tie Phainon to the tree now step to restrain her withered body. “Audata, please,” one of them says. “You know what must be done.”

His mother looked much older than her sixty years. Grief patterns itself into the wrinkles of her face; lines for her own sister, lost when they were only babe. Lines for her husband, Phainon’s father, who had not seen his son turn ten.

If she had not suffered such muscle pain from her years of hunting, she might have been able to cast aside the two men who leverage her now. As it was, all she can do is collapse to the ground as her sobs shatter the quiet air. They drift away as she is carried from the clearing. Phainon knows he will never see her again. It brings him selfish comfort to know that at least one mourned his forever going, even if he would be forgotten by dawn, accepted as a loss they needed to overcome for the safety of all that there was. He had not been close to her, though desperately wished he had. She had gone so far-away after his father passed into the shadows and they sent his body down the river at nighttime that she had hardly looked at him again, for all of these past years until now.

There is no ceremony, no great trial or parade. Those who have bound him light a single wax candle before him, a pinprick of light in the slow-falling night. It flickers as darkness engulfs the trees and weeping willow stalks around him, so it might seem as though each is a hand striking through the darkness, seeking to take him but never able to grasp firmly his taught limbs or heaving chest.

It is a long time before it appears. There he waits, brushed by the spindly fingers of the branches about him, praying to a stagnant water-lily wind. Alone.

The candle flickers. Once. Twice. Snuffed out not by a breeze, but by a sudden stillness of the air. A great silence approached; greater than any before or after, greater than the foggy stars, or cold, cold earth that stretched beneath his bare feet.

About him the shadows bend and merge and fold into each other. And from them, in an instant so vast Phainon cannot perceive it, it is there.

It. The thing. The creature.

What Phainon expected he did not know. Perhaps a great monster, gnarled and ugly as the roots of an old oak tree. Perhaps a great divinity, a heavenly being too bright for him to comprehend, unable even to be considered in words or thought or feeling.

Instead, across the clearing where he was bound, he sees it in the shape of a man.

What it wears is lost to the shadows it is still half-draped in, but its hair is bright and wild and free, blonde-red curls framing its face as the lilies about the river did the grass. And oh, its face. Something great rises in Phainon at the sight of it, something the earth and sky and air tells him is truer than they are, more ancient than they are, more important than they could ever be.

It was beautiful.

From across the ten paces between them bleeds a hunger woven into the air, strung about on the late spring breeze, dancing between each breath Phainon takes regarding such beauty before him. It is a hunger so great it eats Phainon alive. A hunger so permeating, so old that it hurts him. His throat burns, and his lungs shrivel and twist and knot, and somehow, for some reason, his body longs to bend to this hunger. This great truth, this infinite pain; to turn his neck in offering, to let himself be devoured as he was born to be.

It takes everything in Phainon to fight it, and yet he does. Fists clenched, jaw set, body tight in its ropes – he refuses to waiver from the stare which threatens to engulf him, swallow him, eat him alive.

He will not give this thing what it wants easily. This oath he has already made to himself; he will be no willing sacrifice. He will be no victim, no hapless offering.

The thing frowns – a hard, unusual movement of its sculpted face, as that perfect brow draws together, its eyes flickering as the candle it put out. The planes of its face are chiselled like the marble columns that lined the village centre, cut cheekbones framing a hooked nose, inhuman eyes startlingly yellow-gold like the sun. It looks to be thinking, hard and slowly, as its mouth comes to open, tasting Phainon and his fear and defiance at one.

“Eat,” it says.

The sound of its voice – deep and hoarse and unused – almost makes Phainon’s knees buckle. So rich a sound, so gravelled and permanent, he wonders if he has always known what such a creature sounds like in his dreams.

And yet Phainon does not waiver.

“No,” Phainon chokes out.

The thing frowns further. In a blink of an eye it is before Phainon, not touching him yet almost pressed flush to his form. Overwhelming, unconscionable hunger eats Phainon from the inside out; he is so empty, so hollow that he must present his neck, he must let this thing feed from him, he must–

Its eyes flicker to Phainon’s lips as they wobble, to his neck where his pulse lays beating and warm, back to his eyes.

“Eat,” it says with more urgency this time. A wave of aching desire washes over Phainon, dousing him in the desperate, compelling urge to obey, to offer his life to a thing far greater than him.

And yet he holds firm.

“No,” he says again. His voice shakes as the leaves in the still trees around them, and they do not reach the night sky.

Now the thing looks angry. Uncontrollable rage bubbles between them, thick and hot like blood, like corpses piled atop each other, like unending darkness beyond the only world there was.

The thing looks at him, truly looks at him, and Phainon cannot stop it as the shadows begin to warp and form from its body, and the humming builds and builds, a great cacophony of screaming and drumming and endless, incomplete silence; it sounds like screaming – no, it feels like screaming, like he is the sound, the never-ending nothing and everything and all of time in one singular point– it is darkness forever, it is all made of shadows, here to the edge of the world– and he goes into them willingly, and he wonders if he will ever wake up.
☾


The clank of a chain jerks him awake.

Body like lead, it feels as though all the shadows themselves have bound to his limbs and dragged them down, and Phainon finds himself staring at the cobbled stone ceiling arched above his head with dizzy abandon. He must be inside the castle atop the hill. No other building in Elysiae looked like this one, with all its fitted stone and grey mortar, and he had spent enough nights staring at the magnificent ruins far away from their village to know the pattern of its brickwork by now.

The chain is not bound to him but to the columned rafters above him, swaying slightly with some shadowy movement. Free-moving and with all his limbs thankfully intact, Phainon sits up and finds he had been put to rest atop a grand bed. Moth-bitten posters hold red fabric aloft in fitted drapery. When Phainon’s hand comes to touch it, the texture is strange enough he grimaces and draws away, for one direction it was smooth and the other like thistle spikes on his skin.

The room was fine-fitted, if a little bare. Dusty. Very dusty, actually. Phainon runs a finger across the headboard and watches the speckles swirl and group in the firelight of the singular oil lamp lit by the bedside. A milky window gives way to empty blackness. Was it nighttime, or was the window barred?

Was this it, then? The place he would be kept; the pen an ancient creature kept its food in?

There he goes about exploring the room curiously, picking apart what he considered his prison with vague intrigue. A tiled washroom sat adjacent to the bedchamber, unlike any he had ever seen before, with a bath and rusted spigots and, in the corner, a great heaping pile of soft things. Piles and piles of fabric, woollen towels and woven throws, thin blankets and ragged pillows, many of them old and creased and torn about the edges. Strange. Pumping the strange copper lever in the sink makes it and all the pipe-work creak, until at last water runs bronze-red with rust though the tap. After some time it glistens clear and sparkling, and Phainon sticks his head beneath the flow and gulps mouthfuls and mouthfuls. It tastes like fresh mountain spring.

The window was barred, he finds, as his fingers creep around the edges of the wooden planks. They seem nailed in from the outside, and he cannot find purchase against them – but a small hole in the damp wood reveals to him it was daytime, if barely.

Nobody comes for him. Certainly not the creature. Phainon cannot even sense it in the shadows or in creeping silence. How alone is he, how vast is this castle that such ancient terror remains out of his reach?

And alone he remains for the better part of the rest of the day, and all the way into quiet, cool night. A draft rushes from beneath the locked door of his cage; it was stone, as the rest of the room, and laced with wooden pillories and bronze barred buckles. There was no give on that, either. Not even a latch that might slip food to him.

He sleeps well in the grand bed, at least, though his stomach grumbles, and in his dreams he sees a great shadow about his village, and no amount of candles lit and waved about ever chase it away.

The next day he trails the room again, fingers pressing into every crack of old stone, every dusty crevice in search of anything at all that might give or reveal some waiting secret. He figures out how to run the bath through the spigot, but not how to scrub the stained grime from its ceramic edge, and eventually he gives up. Now he was famished, hunger gnawing at his empty stomach, the water doing little to fill him. Would the creature return soon? Would Phainon be given food only if he became it first?

Night crept once more through the single draft in the shuttered window. Enough, he thinks. He needed something to eat.

“Hello?” he calls, banging on the door. It echoes through what he can only imagine to be an empty, dark corridor, and nothing comes in response. “Hello? Creature? Thing?”

When the nothingness drags on despite his calling, Phainon kicks the bed and shakes the posters until stone dust rains from the ceiling, and stomps about the rooms with heavy feet.

Silence.

Great and gaping and terrifying and hollow; it opens before him, spreads over his skin like a mould. Dread and anticipation rise as the bursting banks of a river. All the shadows of his singular oil lamp suddenly bend and warp and come together on the floor, dancing about in a concentric flame until it appears before him.

It. The creature. Now Phainon can see it is dressed strangely; black slacks and a woven white shirt with frills about its neck, torn and ragged and long dirty. Circling its limbs were bright red marks the colour of freshly pricked blood, painting all of its body in strange, geometric designs. Markings of a beast, Phainon thinks, though he knows not what they truly are.

This thing was so beautiful, and terrifying, and nothing and everything all at once that it steals Phainon’s breath from him once more. Yet when Phainon tried to focus on its face his gaze slips from its features like water, unable to recall many features besides its overwhelming handsomeness. Its shoulders were certainly wide and strong, and when Phainon’s stare travels over the tight muscle rising up and around its neck and arms, he has to cast his eyes back to his slippery face in the hope something there might distract him.

It worked, for somehow the thing managed to appear contemptuous as it stared at Phainon. Despite all its ancient beauty, the great draw of its power, the unending hunger which radiated from its form; this thing was annoyed.

“Noisy,” it says, nose wrinkled, clearly displeased with Phainon’s racket.

“So you do know more words than eat,” Phainon replies.

The creature narrows its eyes at him, but waits. As though to prove its inhuman being, its eyes do not flicker as humans might, dancing about the room to see what it wished. Instead the shadows sought for it, ripping from every corner, pulsing with their desire to taste every corner of the bedchamber in its stead.

“I need food,” Phainon says eventually, when it is clear the other thing will give him nothing in return.

The thing does not move. It stares blankly at him, and blinks once.

Phainon points to himself. “Eat.”

Suddenly the creature is before him, the shadows propelling him faster than any sight might comprehend. A great wave of hunger compels Phainon’s knees to bend, his neck to bare and hands open to grasp the other; he fights it as best he can, even at the sudden shining spark in the creature's starving eyes. It nods, enthusiastic.

“Yes,” it almost drawls, tongue flickering out to wet his lips. “Eat.”

“No,” Phainon manages to choke out, and steps back once. The distance eases his body's sudden terror and the deep, purple feeling in his gut. “I need to eat. Me.”

The thing stares at him, blank and confused. Phainon could almost watch it think. The oil lamp dances between them both.

“If I don’t eat, I will die,” Phainon says. As though to emphasise his point, his stomach rumbles.

At that, all the shadows bend and twist in the creature's sudden panic. Clearly upset, the stricken being takes three quick steps backwards, and then the shadows absorb it entirely.

It is gone.

Another day passes. The creature does not reappear, but Phainon does not call for it again. Perhaps he might starve to death, and honestly he does not mind the thought of it much. What sacrifice would they send next? How might they placate this thing, this terrible ancient being, if it would not feed from him?

Was Phainon doing something wrong? Was he not to this things liking - would it have preferred another maiden to take? The thought almost offended him, though he doesn’t understand why. Phainon was big. He was tall, perhaps even taller than this thing. If it did not want a girl anymore, then it had gotten its wish.

For a creature so old, so ancient as they knew it to be; it had seemed somehow both confused and young when presented with Phainon imminent mortality. Unsure and afraid and nothing like an all-knowing, terrifying protector.

When Phainon wakes the next day, it is to the sight of blood.

Fear rakes through him at the scene on the floor of the room which confines him. All the air is thick with it, the scent of iron and the steady, singular drip of something wet against cold stone.

A deer. Its great brown carcass is laid across the carved stone and still hummed with warmth. As Phainon watches the blood seeps from its neck – not where it had been cut, but where it had been gouged by inhumanly sharp teeth, torn muscle and tendon oozing thick, glistening scarlett.

All Phainon can do is stare at it, woollen covers drawn up to his chest. The poor animal's beady eye is fixed on him just like the bull, and does not move in death.

Was this… a way to test him? To scare him? To show him what happens if he continues to refuse to give his blood? Phainon did not know why the thing did not eat him of its own accord. It could so easily take whatever he wanted, filled with such ancient and unyielding power as it was.

He cannot stand to look at the carcass. Hunting occurred often in the village, the women sent to set traps or track the pitted prints of the game through the underbrush of the forest which surrounded their riverside village. But Phainon himself had never warmed to the activity. Watching life leave another, using it for one’s own gain; it never felt right inside of him. So he takes one of the many blankets shoved into the corner of the washroom, unfolds it, and covers the deer with a wrinkled nose.

The next day when he wakes once more, it is a different sight that awaits him, but one no less gruesome or bloody.

The deer was gone, as was the blood-sodden blanket. Now, in its place, was a sheep. Its matted wool hung in clumps from the open wound in its neck that pumped little rivers of fresh blood through the seams of the stone floor.

Still, Phainon covers it with yet another blanket. Still, he fears what it means.

So that third day Phainon sits awake all night. He waits, and he waits, and pinches his skin whenever the exhaustion threatens to consume him, or walks about the room to shake the tiredness from his limbs and bend and stretch and remain painfully conscious.

When the shadows warp and twist and all the silence in the world condenses into a spot so heavy it begins to scream though no sound comes; it appears. The creature.

Its mouth is drenched in rich blood, coating its simple clothing as though stained with wine, glistening thick and wet with shredded slices of tendon and sinew. And in its arms it holds, as though light as a feather, a great wolf, white of pelt and beautiful, limp where the creature had torn out its neck.

“Are you trying to scare me?”

The creature almost seems surprised. It jumps, the shadows at its feet retreating in fear, and stares at Phainon. Blood drips from its stilled mouth and hits the floor with a wet slap. It does not swallow it, or chase the taste from its lips.

“I know you can kill. You do not have to scare me.” Phainon gestures at the wolf with a grimace. “If you want to feed from me, just do it. Don’t threaten me with my village's livestock, or wild animals from the edges of the shadow boundary. I understand you are hungry. That is why I was given to you.”

The creature looks at him. It looks at the wolf, and the sheep on the floor, now beginning to sag and smell beneath its wool cover.

“Eat,” it says.

“I do not want you to eat me.” Phainon’s voice waivers but he holds firm. “So I– I will keep saying no. But you can do it anyway, can’t you? So just get it over with. Please.”

Slowly, Phainon stretches his neck before them both. Bares it to this thing, naked and thudding as his pulse was in his ears. Better him than another bull from his village. Better him than any other human besides.

The thing blinks. Though its gaze flickers to Phainon’s bared neck, it does not move towards him.

Instead it holds out its arms, offering him the wolf.

“No. You said, need food.” The words seem strange to it, all foreign and twisted, and it clearly takes great effort to form them. “Find food for human. So human eat.”

Phainon stares at it. His neck stops stretching. His brow furrows.

Oh.

Is this what all the previous sacrifices have eaten for all of these years? Slaughtered livestock, raw in this room?

Surely not? Surely they would grow sick and wither and die long before decades pass?

Did being fed from such an ancient power sustain a human in some way? Could it? Oh, how terribly confused Phainon feels suddenly. All of the terror of his situation flees him, and is replaced, instead, by unsettling nausea.

“Human does not like wolf?” grumbles the creature suddenly, shoulders slumping in defeat. “Human does not like sheep. Human does not like deer. Picky and noisy, human.” It huffs in annoyance once again. Despite its great power, the great abscess of its existence, such an action was almost endearing.

“I cannot eat these things,” Phainon says, and almost feels bad for such an inconvenience.

The thing frowns.

Phainon points at his chest. “Human will get sick. Human will die. Cannot eat dead human.”

The thing, at that, panics once more. The shadows bend and warp with vigour, and it is gone along with the livestock, leaving only a wine-dark stained floor behind.

Another two days pass. Phainon thought he would be content with starving to death, for at least it was a manner of dying that left him some autonomy in his suffering, but the hunger begins to wrack him with too much pain to bear. He picks through the seams of the tapestry-draped stonewall, thinking the soft mossy mulch might at least do something should he lick it from the wet brick, but it is not so bad as he might bring himself to try, only stare at it longingly. Then he scrubs the floor with a rugged blanket when the sight of the blood makes him nauseous, and grows so tired he sleeps on the floor still as the dead for the whole night. When he wakes, it is all he can do in his weakness to stare at the stone brick ceiling and sigh. Surely this thing, this creature, could not have so little knowledge on keeping a human? It had haunted them for centuries. It had kept each girl they gave it alive for almost a century each time.

He must slip into unconsciousness, for when he wakes again with a start, it is to the mouthwatering smell of fresh bread.

The creature stood above him. In its hand is a great loaf of fresh, warm bread, and the other juggles a linen-wrapped bundle of jam and jar of pressed orange juice.

Without speaking, Phainon pounces on the food where the creature sets it down by his feet. Still warm on his fingertips, the fluffy, seeded bread tears with a wonderful crackling sound, and Phainon devours it with little care for etiquette. It melts on the tongue just as Granna Noma’s did in the village. The pear jam – which he does not even bother to dip the bread in, just smears it on his finger and shoves it into his mouth to compliment the sodden pastry – is sweet and tart as it pops on his tongue, and he glugs the pressed orange juice to chase it down with an embarrassing moan.

Hunger. Hunger greater than any other before bears down on him suddenly, and he hunches under the weight of it, choking on his thick bite of bread. Such a feeling was so sudden and so great it was hunger named longing, named desire, named lust.

Phainon clears his throat with a cough, and drags his eyes up to the one radiating such hunger before him. The creature stood far away, rocking on the balls of its feet as it devoured the sight of Phainon eating with those bright, burning, inhuman eyes.

Phainon offers the remaining half of the bread.

The thing blinks. Stares at the loaf with a strange longing, and shakes head.

“Mydeimos will get sick,” it says, parroting Phainon’s sentence structure from a few days before.

“Mydeimos?” Phainon asks through another mouthful of sticky jam. He looks upon the creature, standing there with its arms hanging by its side, and is struck suddenly by how human its form was. “That is your name?”

It was a strange name. Certainly not one Phainon had ever heard before, though there were not many names in the village, for most sons were named after their grandfathers, and most daughters after their grandmothers, so the cycle was unending with each generation, and all knew which family they came from in the very beginning.

And yet it nods. Once.

“She gave it me,” he says, as though that was a clear explanation.

Him.

Mydei had talked of another. Another creature like him? Another vampire? Until now Phainon had assumed the other was a human, but that did not make much sense if he had managed to forbid Mydei of all things to speak or drink another's blood.

Perhaps, once, there had been two vampires. Perhaps something had occurred with the last sacrifice, and that was why the other girl the village had tried to give to Mydei had been rejected. Now Mydei was in charge of their food, he wished for it to fit his tastes instead, and had chosen a man rather than a woman to feed upon.

“What do you think?” Phainon grins, motioning at the set table as Mydei appears that evening with his food – a steaming bowl of potato leek soup and, for some strange reason, a half-full jug of ale.

Worry steaks Mydei's face as he glances about the set table. “This is… how humans eat?”

Phainon nods, devouring the food with no hesitation where he sits at the head of the table draped in the light of the candles. “We do it often in the village, where everyone cooks for each other, and we gather about for supper. Eating together, enjoying the meal – sometimes someone might sing, or we set up a fire in the square and dance about it before our bellies are too full.”

Mydei does not say anything to this. He stares at Phainon’s throat when he swallows, and keeps in silence for the rest of the meal. As always, when Phainon is finished, the vampire disappears with the empty bowl and jug. Phainon feels the great silent stare watching him from the shadows as he treks back to his bedroom until he shuts the door behind him and readies for sleep.
☾


The charcoal scratches grow faster than he cares to notice – fifty-one – for Phainon, now, had a world to explore. Over the next few weeks he maps the entire library, re-binds the burnt torches and fixes them to the braziers as he goes, so he might light his way through the labyrinth of words every time he went.

He does not light all the torches. He leaves a darkness, always, somewhere behind him. For that is where he feels the stare, wrapped in shadow and shining as the sun, watching him sit in silent awe flick through every book and scroll and tome. Mydei does not let him go about the castle on his own, but Phainon wonders if Mydei knows that he can feel the vampire's presence, or if the vampire, somehow, thinks he blends in entirely with the shadows and makes no ripples in the darkness at all.

Whatever the case, Phainon has decided that his hypothesis must be correct. He trails the shelves for books with the names of places mentioned - Dolos and Okhema and The Grove - and finds more and more books and scrolls written strangely about all manner of things and places and peoples, as though what they professed to tell one was the absolute truth.

Once, the world had been huge. He knows this, now. For who might write all these words, and who might read them, unless there were people in more numbers than five dozen? And Mydei, in all the power he radiated, the sinking of the earth, the great expanse of sky; he clearly did not read these books, for the layers and layers of dust about them. So that meant the person who collected these books must have been to these places, and Phainon thinks that person might be ‘him,’ though he was no close to discovering who he was besides.

Now in the evenings, as Phainon eats his one meal, Mydei sits across from him. First he had stood a little too close, and all the great power about him had gathered and pulsed and settled like dew on the floor, and Phainon had found it hard to swallow when staring at the beauty of such a strange being. So he had told Mydei to sit if he were to watch. For some reason the vampire listened to him.

“Where do you get all this food anyway?” Phainon asks around a mouthful of bread that dusk, dipping it in the tomato broth, watching the foam melt into the soft loaf and wetting it with his tongue.

“Village,” Mydei says simply from across the dining table.

Phainon almost spits out his bread.

“The village? Aedes Elysiae?”

The vampire frowns. “Do you know another village?”

Phainon stares at the loaf in his hand in horror. No wonder it tasted like Granny Noma's bread. It was her bread! Stolen from beneath her nose, fresh out of her old stone oven, ready to be eaten by all the village children as they ran and played and gathered water from the well.

Oh, dear. What state would the village be in now, that human food might begin to go missing from it?

“You just… appear, and steal it?” Phainon asks, entirely incredulous.

The vampire stares at him. His hair is wild like the flicker of candlelight that frames his face. “Yes. Humans not see if not looking.”

“Oh, shadows and all. Stop it, Mydei. Please. Do not steal from the village again.”

“But… if you do not eat, you will die. You said.”

Phainon sets his bread on the plate, swallowing about it with unease. “I will- I will figure something out. Just promise me you will not do it again. Please, Mydei. Food in the village is hard to make, and harder even to come by.”

Mydei’s brow draws together. Those golden eyes rake the human over again, seeing him, studying him; what he finds on Phainon’s face clearly upsets him, and he nods solemnly.

“I understand, human Phainon,” he says, utterly sincere. “I promise. I am… sorry.”

Phainon tells him it is alright for he did not know, but Mydei’s face remains troubled as a storm, and dinner is finished in silence.

The next day, with much determination, Phainon begins further exploration of the castle, resolved to map beyond the grand library that had grasped his attention for so long. If there had been another living here, someone with a dining table that could sit dozens, and if the sacrifices their village had given over the years had lived past two weeks, there must surely be some human food in the castle, pasty and gruel-like as Phainon imagines it to be.

Locked door follows locked door. The echoing rattle of Phainon’s exploration dances down the empty halls as though mocking him with laughter. When he ghosts his fingers on the floor beneath each archway, no cold air reaches his skin. Dead ends.

But eventually, after a day and a half of searching, his stomach rumbling and his oil lamp beginning to run low, Phainon finally happens upon it.

A kitchen.

It was huge, made with hemmed stone and with a fresh tinge to the air unlike the rest of the palace. A larder led into a counter top workspace and stone oven and- oh, Phainon could sing for joy, a pantry almost as large as the library stocked with food to its low ceiling. Human food! Corridors on end of dried wheat and barley in great woven sacks, preserved jams and glazes in shining glass jars, and all manner of sugars and salts and spices Phainon could not name and had no idea where they came from. All were foods that should last many decades dry and kept safe. And such food had clearly been there a long time already – but he places a dye rye oat on his tongue and grinds it with his teeth, and finds it all seemed preserved well enough to eat; though he would have to throw out most of the dried fruits, sticky and rotten as they had become lining two entire shelves.

A book sits on the vast stone counter top by a lonely pestle and mortar. After the sink spills sweet spring water with a few pumps of the spigot, Phainon rolls up his tunic sleeves and scrubs at the sides with a rag he finds under the basin. There too he discovered a ratty old apron and he wraps it about his stomach before opening the book and propping it on the side.

Recipes. Human recipes.

Each was painstakingly illustrated with beautiful ink diagrams that glitter in the firelight as though printed stars. Phainon is quick to set about to work. As he gathers the ingredients from the pantry and lays them out, dusting and cleaning and tasting as he goes, it is not long before he is beading sweat on his brow, kneading a batch of cream-coloured dough that grows stretchy and warm in his palms.

When he comes to the stone oven, despite his laying about of the very dry twigs, he cannot tilt his oil lamp enough to catch the fire, nor can he reach in to grab them for how far down they lie. He sits back on his haunches for a moment and considers hurrying back to the library to pick a torch from the wall, when suddenly a crackle and blast of heat leave him scrambling backwards. Before him a great flame roars to life, almost singing his eyebrows with its force.

Phainon gawks at it, this sudden fire, and realises the stare on his back is just as hot as the flames before him. When he hurries to his feet and turns, Mydei stands in the middle of the kitchen, arms hanging by his side, white shirt yellow in the flames.

“Give human fire,” he says helpfully.

“You– you control fire, too?” Phainon gawks.

Mydei frowns, clearly displeased. “Mydeimos controls nothing. Only asks nicely for shadows to leave. They listen to me. Not to you.”

“Oh. I see,” Phainon says, though he clearly does not. Still, he grins, hoping his human charm might assure this creature of his innocence. “Well. However you did it, thank you anyway, Mydei.”

Then with careful tempering he brings the fire to smouldering embers beneath the pulsing heat of the stone oven, causing the air to shimmer with its heat. When he returns to the worktop and begins to flatten the dough, he nods at the vampire still standing there and back to his kneading hands.

“You can watch me, if you want–”

Phainon cannot finish his sentence. In an instant the shadows have bent and Mydei is hovering behind him, breathing loud in his ear, almost pressed flush his back.

Such proximity fills Phainon with a sudden and terrible desire, with a gaping, silent hunger, with pressing aching need. This Mydei was so close to him, so desperately close, and there is a hunger greater than all, a darkness greater than all–

Pointedly ignoring it and the creature behind him, Phainon swallows the lump in his throat and douses his hands in flour to knead once again. Grinds the dry pumpkin seed in the pestle and mortar, then sprinkles a few poppy-seed stems and wheat flaxen into the bread, but he hardly focuses on what he is doing, for the cold breath that lingers on his neck, the intense ancient power that envelops his entire back.

Mydei breathed. Or at least he appeared to breathe, the ghost of an action he did not need but followed through regardless. How very strange.

“How do you know what is next to do?” the vampire asks suddenly, voice right by Phainon’s ear as his calloused hands press the dough into pocketed loaves.

Phainon points towards the book and illustrations. “The instructions are quite convoluted, but if you follow the pictures, it works well. I’m not the best cook really, but I can make a good rye loaf, and it is my favourite.”

When the bread is baked, turned over twice in the oven until the crust is shiny and brown, Phainon sets half aside for a noon meal the next day and gathers the rest on a cloudy copper platter by a parcelled pot of jam spread and marmalade. There he goes to sit in the dining room once more. Mydei sticks close to him the whole time, intense gaze focused, completely and utterly, on Phainon and his hands as he worked.

Finding such large quantities of human food like that, squirrelled away in some vast cellar pantry, arose far more questions than answers. Of course the sacrifices had to be fed somehow, but Phainon had never given it much thought; how a woman was kept alive for eighty years in the castle of some ancient being. And as Phainon woke the next day to etch a charcoal line on the wall - sixty four - he thinks not only of this question, but all the rest he still does not know.

Why had the shadows eaten the world? Why was Aedes Elysiae the only place left? Who else used to live in this castle – who owned all the books in the world, and where did he go?

That day Phainon spends scouring the library, fingering through each volume title, set to create a pile of books that might mention the word vampire at all. There were not many. In the dozen shelves he manages to get through before the air is tinged with cold evening, he finds only two. One is a wax-stamped scroll of which the contents spell a rhyming limerick of all the different ways a vampire might bite.

But the other is far stranger. A thin, string-bound collection of hand written letters, signed only by an initial - Σ. It spoke not of the danger of ancient powers, not of the terror and silence and pure, unrestrained enmity an ancient, immortal being might wield; none of the sort.

It detailed, quite graphically, the lurid ecstasy this Σ had experienced after letting a vampire feed from them.

Words Phainon had never encountered before spoke of the complete and utter orgasmic pleasure a human would receive when giving part of themselves up for a greater being than they, subsisting an immortal creation and linking themselves with another life form through blood. The blinding fire it settled in one’s gut, the constant and beautiful need that wove itself into one’s very soul should they choose to sustain the heavenly beauty of a vampire.

What a wonder it was, to submit oneself to the most ancient form of power. Nature agreed, for I have never felt such blinding desire as when my beloved Helektra latched to my neck, and in that moment my arrival shook my body to its very core, and the coral and stone about us was wet with my pleasure and blood–

Phainon sets down the letter quickly, face suddenly burning much as the stone oven had when tended to by flame. He folds it up, again and again, this first page and a few of the rest, and shoves them deep into the cord belt of his slacks, though why he keeps them he does not know.

Eventually, stomach grumbling and face flushed and letters burning a hole in his hip, he sets off for the kitchen come evening, oil lamp in hand, desperately trying not to picture the moaning, writhing bodies he had just read about so shamelessly.

Yet even in this, he is halted quite abruptly.

The light flickers from the kitchen; the glow of a tempered fire, licking across the stone floor, bathing the bleak corridor in a sunset haze. Slowly, Phainon inches closer – and realises only then that the shadows had not watched him read today. Mydei had been elsewhere.

Mydei was here.

Hovering above the stove, inhumanely still as he watched the bread in the open oven brown with golden crust. He wore that moth-bitten apron about his strange clothes, and for some reason he had found embroidered gloves, too, though Phainon doubted the heat would impact his immortal body. Scattered about the working surface were a myriad of bowls, pockets of kneaded dough and used measuring spoons. Flour dust his mane of hair like the rare frost Aedes Elysiae sometimes saw in the winter months.

Mydei pokes the bread with his mittens. Once. Twice. He huffs, impatient, and turns instead back to the book, flicking through the page with a rogue shadow and peering at the final ink drawing of sliced bread. He picks through the knives displayed neatly until he finds one as the picture, holding it up to check it is correct, and then studies the jam jar before the shadows bend and Phainon can only hear the clinking of glass far in the pantry.

And Phainon sees the loaf, browning in the oven. Rye and poppy-seed. His favourite.

He returns to the library, for he does not know what else to do. Mydei had not noticed him, though the other clearly had senses far more acute than any human. And Phainon did not want to interrupt him, strange as the behaviour was.

Eventually, as he flips through a book he does not care for with unseeing eyes, the shadows bend, creeping closer and closer all about the library – Mydei, searching for him. Then suddenly he appears, smelling of fresh baking, flour still in his hair.

“Human dinner ready,” he says, and is gone.

So Phainon goes to the grand hall dining room, where the table is laid far more neatly than Phainon had made it up, draped in a mottled cream tablecloth with candles lit in their golden stands dusted and shining with smears of wet polish. At the head of the table where Phainon liked to sit was a loaf of rye bread set on a platter, neatly sliced twice and surrounded by the entremets of jam and dipping palette just as it had been in the glittering book illustration.

“You made this?” Phainon asks as he sits down, though he knows the answer.

Mydei nods purposefully. “Yes. Like the book. Human dinner for human Phainon.”

“It's incredible,” he tells the vampire, and he means it. When he breaks the bread with his hands, he might groan for the plush filling, far softer and fluffier than he might ever make. “Oh, in the shadow's name. Thank you, Mydeimos. Really.”

Mydei blinks at him. “You are welcome, human Phainon.”

“You can just call me Phainon, you know.”

“I know.”

There Phainon takes to devouring the meal in the silence, much unable to control the awe-stricken humming about such delicious, still warm food. Throughout it all Mydei watches from the opposing seat, all the way at the other end of the table, those ancient, golden eyes devouring their own type of meal.

And though Phainon had been desperately trying not to think of it, Mydei was beautiful. Beautiful in a terrifying, inhuman way. In a way that made all his body thrum with deep-seated, new desire, shining like a thousand gemstones tossed into the sun-lit air. And when Phainon forced himself to look past the defence about the vampire, the strange shimmer that made him want to encounter anything but at his beauty, Phainon finds himself looking into the face of a man who was handsome and pretty both. His eyelashes were thick and wheat-yellow as his wild hair, his hooked nose and chiselled jaw set against marble-smooth brown skin. The marking below his eye was bright-blood red. The plush of his lips was pinkish and wet.

“Do you… want to sit closer? To eat with me?” Phainon asks suddenly, unable to bite back the suggestion before it was laid bare.

Mydei frowns his endearing frown. “You said humans sit like this when eating dinner. And also, I cannot eat.”

“I know.” Phainon pokes his bread, and the hunger in the room crests. “But you made it. I can describe it to you. What eating is like, if you want. If you sit close to me.”

A silence swells. Mydei looks between Phainon and his food as though it all might be playing a trick on him.

Then the room sighs. In a soft breeze of air, Mydei is suddenly sat beside Phainon, the oak-backed chair drawn neatly up to the table, their knees almost touching. It is clear the vampire is uncomfortable or unused to sitting, for his back was too straight and face too unfeeling, and for a moment Phainon thinks it was a terrible idea to invite him, because he is filled mightily with a great hunger and a darkness and it never ends and it never ends–

Phainon shakes his head. With enough force he can keep at bay the cloud of hunger hanging about this vampire, and he chooses in that moment to hold up the half-loaf of bread, show Mydei how he tears it apart and dips it in strawberry jam. Mydei’s eyes follow his fingers with unflinching desire, tracking every infinite movement as Phainon takes a soft bite, as he kneads the sweet taste on his tongue and chews the soft dough.

Phainon covers his mouth as he goes to explain the sensation to the other. “It is warm, still, and a little moist–”

Yet he cannot finish.

For there, grasping his wrist, is Mydei’s hand.

Stillness fills him, welling up in him all of a sudden, all the belly of the earth and the vast stretch of sky one and the same; every part of the remaining world concentrating on the singular point of their touch. About them the air hums and the rafters whistle and the food before them sits forgotten.

Mydei’s hand was smooth, and soft, and cold. Pleasantly cold, as the river in spring splashed on one’s face in humid summer, as flipping one’s feather-pillow over to settle into the untouched fabric before sleep. And though the hold was light, it was firm, and concealed barely the raw strength hidden in the body of this vampire.

“No,” Mydei says eventually, dragging Phainon’s hand down to his lap. “Let me watch you, like you said. Or you are a liar, human Phainon. And shadows like liars less than shouting men. Eat.”

Phainon swallows and nods in one. Though Mydei peels his fingers away, Phainon cannot stop the beat of his heart pounding in his ears. Surely the vampire must hear how terribly fast his pulse thuds, how his hands move now with a shakiness they did not possess before. Regardless, Phainon takes another slow bite, now dipping the crust in the hot water infused with dried dates, and speaks openly as he chews.

“It is like… like pressing your fingers to dew grass, with the texture,” he explains as he swallows loudly. “The seeds- they look like they should be gritty, but they add a texture that pops in your mouth and- and sort of coats your tongue, and–”

On and on he describes each bite, each sliver of wet jam, each crackling crunch of perfectly browned crust. And throughout it all Mydei listens, rapt. His intense stare never waivers from Phainon’s mouth, the curve of his neck, the thick swallow of his jaw. At one point his tongue comes to poke his lower lip and wet it with desire, and Phainon feels the great need to bare his neck as he had all those times before and this time tell the vampire it could feast from him too.

He does not. But he feels it all the same.
☾


Now Phainon cannot shake it. As he marks the charcoal on the wall – seventy-three – and as he cleans his face and old tunic in the silk and glances himself in the hammered copper mirror in the washroom, he cannot help it.

In the sparks of the metal he sees gold. Golden eyes, intense and inhuman and terribly ancient, only a pace in front of him as he talks at length about each of his dinners. Yellow in the mottled rot about some of the crinkled pages of the library, yellow like curly hair all about a handsome face, tangled and matted and still flecked with flour and dry blood.

For Mydei clearly loved listening to Phainon describe his eating, and did so each night since the first, hurrying to sit in front of Phainon and watch him with rapt pleasure. And Phainon must always swallow the lump in his throat before he begins to eat, the strange and unwanted desire he feels bubbling away somewhere inside him, right besides his freshly baked bread and seeped tea.

Sitting in the library, in the darkness, Phainon sets the lantern by his feet and settles on one of the many patterned rugs. No matter how much he tried to focus only on the reading of any other book, he kept coming back to the letters the moment Mydei's prying gaze dissipated from the shadows so the vampire might make his dinner. Phainon unfolds one of the letters from his belt and reads it as he has many times since he discovered it. Fingers skimming the long-bled black ink, tracing the words until they were printed into his skin.

One can hardly picture it, the naked body of a human and an immortal being, each the perfect half of a life cycle; the feeding of one’s blood, the giving up of life willingly for the undead. Such excess of blood from the wounds caused by the sharpened teeth of the immortal smear upon one’s skin, and the power infused in their saliva seals the desire deep within one. It is wonderful- nay, heavenly! - the contrast of hot blood against a cold, unfeeling body, the carnal passion of pain with the tender love of dependence. I need no touch to reach my climax, how pure a passion it is. Our legs move together, in perfect time, and the heady arousal that fills her body as she feeds, she tells me, is much like a human orgasm, if even more elevated in pleasure. I should think, with Helektra by my side, I need not conquer or pillage or enslave any longer; for I am a slave myself to the basest of all mortal desires, and I do not seek any other manner of living anymore.

Though the library was quiet and still in its coldness, heat prickles Phainon's body as a fire caught on stoked coals; slowly, then all at once.

He had taken to carrying them around, these letters, though surely it made him a bad person to keep such lurid words on his person all the time. He cannot help it.

And Phainon had never given much thought to partners or sex, really. He sort of assumed it would be like the rest of the village. One day he would get married, and that marriage would be to a woman, and somehow they would have children, and that would be that. He would go about the world as he always had, drifting between what he must do and what was expected of him. Perhaps his mother would smile at him on his wedding day, draped in the netting veil with his wife. Perhaps she might even take him in a hug.

Yet even as he grew up, no matter how much he tried, Phainon felt little towards women, pretty as they were and always nice as they seemed. They came to him often with braided reed-bracelets or stone pins for his hair. He was meant to wear them to accept their courting, though he never had. For when his wandering hands had touched himself as a teenager, as he managed to find time alone far along the riverbank when he was meant to be washing laundry downstream, he had never admitted even to himself that what he saw in his mind was no girl at his side, but maybe someone with a flattened chest, with broad shoulders, with a rumbling voice below his own chasing hips–

He cannot help himself when he dines either. Now his stare lingers on Mydei in a similar way; tracing his wild hair, his sharp eyes, his pink-plush lips and beautiful hooked nose. Wonders what this creature might look like lying by his side, and if in the heat of the moment his cold, inhuman body would be a comfort to Phainon’s hot-blooded humanness. Perhaps the power made the vampire purposefully as he was; beautiful, so his prey might seek his touch. This Σ had certainly spoken as though the act of giving one’s blood completed her, made her feel whole in no way any act of human desire might compare.

At least Mydei seemed completely unaware of his powerful draw, sitting on his chair with their knees almost touching, patiently waiting for Phainon to begin his description of eating as he did every evening.

“Do you want to feel me swallow?” Phainon asks suddenly.

Where the blunt question comes from, rising all in him and tangling in his mouth, he does not know. Mydei stares at him. Those golden eyes flicker to Phainon’s throat and back up to his face. Once. Twice.

Slowly, Phainon reaches out. Lets his fingers ghost the back of Mydei's hand, circling the red diamond printed into the surface. Then he grasps the it entirely. Mydei does not move, still as the mirrored surface of a well barred from falling rain. And Mydei’s hand was still cold and smooth like stone, but surprisingly supple as Phainon flattens the vampire’s fingers slowly then brings them up to his own throat.

Feeling the pulse beneath his freckled skin, the movement of the blood he craved so, Mydei gulps loudly, nostrils flaring and eyes sparking. With the vampire’s hand against his throat Phainon takes a bite of bread and chews slowly – and when he swallows, he makes sure to do it with great artifice, pushing his throat forward and letting his neck bob with the force of it.

A sound.

Startling and deep like the great growl of a hunting wolf that had Phainon suddenly upright and alert.

But Mydei does not flinch. And Phainon realises the sound was Mydei, and it was not a growl but more of a moan, a longing, a lust.

“Eat,” the vampire says as though to himself. But when Phainon does not respond, he looks up, frustrated and impatient. “Eat,” he urges. His eyes have glazed over, taking on a sheen of carnal desperation, an animalistic longing far greater than any mortal might comprehend.

Phainon takes another bite.

Mydei’s hand comes to cup his throat entirely. His finger presses into the soft spongy skin beneath Phainon’s chin, right in the divot of his jaw, so he might feel Phainon’s tongue poke and prod each bite. His fingers fan his jaw and neck and his palm presses flat against the apple of his throat, sensing both the thud of his pulse and heave of his swallow. A strength greater than any human, great enough to crush Phainon’s throat in a single move, is held back only by the vampires' barely tempered restraint.

Something red settles deep in Phainon's gut. Another bite, and another. Mydei is leant forward on his chair now, hardly sitting at all. An intense stare rests on Phainon’s mouth, on its biting and chewing and moving. When Phainon licks his own lips, Mydei mirrors the action, chasing the plush of his bottom lip about with a wet tongue.

Wet. Mydei’s tongue was wet. Phainon does not really know why he notices again. He knew this, didn’t he? Why did it matter now?

For a moment, it is just this. Just a human eating, and a vampire watching, feeling Phainon eat through the palm of his hand. A shift of Mydei's fingers draws them over Phainon’s chin, to tug and pull at his lips as they move.

And Phainon leans down.

It is all caught in him, the reasons for why he moves, and he does not care in the moment to sort them out. All he knows is that he dips his jaw downwards so his open lips might take the vampire’s fingers into his mouth, thread them one to the side of his gnashing teeth and the other to press the roll of his tongue.

And Mydei makes that sound again. That deep, wanting moan, rumbled as thunder, purple as a polished pearl. His fingers, cold in Phainon’s mouth against the hot food he ate, probe Phainon’s tongue. They stroke the muscle as it swallows, and Phainon has to hold back the gag from how far suddenly they force their way inside him, how wet and sodden his chin feels from chewing with his mouth half open.

It is strange. It should not be happening. Neither of them seem to act on this knowledge, though, and whether Mydei understood this to be odd was clearly of no concern to the immortal. Instead, his fingers knead and work the food in time with Phainon’s chewing, and care little for when the teeth bite at his skin, stiff and marble-like as it felt when Phainon did. When the meal is finished, neither of them move. They are locked in a trance; Mydei staring at Phainon’s mouth, and Phainon at Mydei’s golden eyes.

So Phainon licks about the fingers in his mouth, closing his lips around them to clean them of the food. Then, though all the earth below them sifts and bemoans the breaking of contact, and the shining gem deep in Phainon’s gut desperately, miserably wants to stay connected to this creature; Phainon pulls backwards. Such an action causes Mydei to jerk backwards suddenly, with those inhumanly fast movements. The fingers disappear from Phainon’s mouth. Mydei does not wipe Phainon’s spit clean on anything, and they glisten wet where the vampire once again sets them neatly on his knees.

“Thank you, human Phainon,” he says quite seriously.

“You… you are welcome,” Phainon manages through the thickening pound of his heart in his ears and the humming of his skin.

“...Hmph.”

Phainon can still feel the fingers heavy in his mouth. “What? Did I… was that alright? For you?”

“Yes. I said thank you,” Mydei says, nose managing to wrinkle in irritation despite what had just happened. “It is just… your heart is very loud, now. It makes me hungrier, for you smell even better. Sweeter, like morning-time. That is all.”

Then the vampire gathers up the plates as he did every meal, and disappears like nothing had happened.

Later, in bed, Phainon’s hand comes to his own throat. Traces where those cold fingers had lay, where the immortal had touched him, held him, felt him. Feeds into his mouth, open and warm and waiting as he holds it, tracing the line of his tongue, mapping the soft pouch of his cheeks.

Now, his body ached. There was an absence where Mydei had been, a desperate craving he could not describe or think to satiate. It follows him into his dreams. It wraps around his throat, and tells him of a darkness greater than all, and a suffering greater than all, and a hunger greater than all.

They could forget Phainon ever existed, though Phainon feels a little like he never existed in the first place. Not really. Not in any way that mattered.

It seemed Phainon a little unfair to force the being making him delicious dinner each evening to divulge information he clearly did not want to dwell on – even if that being was also an undying vampire who held Phaino captive in the desperate hope one day he could be eaten.

Each day he went about the library thumbing through every book and scroll for information about the vast world there once was. The first time he gives Phainon soup with a side of toasted bread dippers and sliced and stewed dried apple, Phainon’s mouth waters so much he has to swallow the lump in his throat before he drools. Each complicated dish – each fruit-oat porridge and intricately plaited bread and potato-bone broth – was always somehow better than the last, warm and hearty where it settled in his stomach, satiating him so well with such wonderful mixtures of savoury and fruit-fresh sweetness.

And each night Mydei sits before him, just to the side of the table, and grasps Phainon’s neck in his hands, and feels the human man eat each bite. When his fingers inevitably come to slip their way into Phainon’s mouth, to stroke the firm muscle of his tongue or probe the softness of his cheeks, Phainon learns quickly the best way to eat around them, and does not mind it.

Really does not mind it. The deep-seated, terrible desire it stirs inside him he ignores, even if all he can picture is Mydei’s tongue against his, eating him, ravaging him–

By the time another week had passed, Mydei's room was an entirely different place. A warm fire crackled almost constantly in the sanded fireplace, and the bed was hung by red drapes and huge plush throws. Phainon had cleaned a rug from the hallway and laid it on the floor, and fitted braziers to the wall so it would not be so dark all the time, and re-boarded the windows so the rotting, damp wood couldn’t leak mulch into the stone and drape mouldy moss down the window-sills.

He left, of course, that sliver of wall where the sunlight fell each day.

“Cannot touch the sun,” Mydei says on what would surely be the last day of the project as Phainon stares, hands on his hips, at the glow of light in deep thought. Mydei sat on the bed once more, hand still clasped about his braid. It was messy, now, pulled from its plait after a week of being grasped; but the vampire kept holding it as though it was precious to him. “It will burn the shadows in me. Pain is… very bad.”

It was clear Mydei was speaking from experience, and something in Phainon ached, though he did not know the story of this creature’s coming about yet. Had Mydei once tried to seek the sun? Had he reached his hand out, seeing such bright, beautiful light, unknowing it would not accept his touch?

So Phainon goes about suddenly from Mydei’s bedchamber, for he knows what he will do and will not hesitate as he might have done once before. He fixtures shards of broken mirror he had dusted from the floor in an empty hallway to a wooden board using sticky dates from the kitchen and charcoal mixed into a sap, that when held to the waving heat of a fire dry the mixture into a hard bark grip, With an old picture frame he creates a lever and pushing mechanism, soldered with dripping candle wax, and fixtures the wooden palette to the sliver of the wall in Mydei’s room where the sunlight might enter with old brazier spigots. All in all, it takes no more than a few hours of tinkering, and then it is set.

“What are you doing now?” Mydei asks him, nose wrinkled, clearly quite tired of Phainon’s meddling in his space.

“Human Phainon was making more sun for vampire Mydeimos,” Phainon tells him with a grin.

And by flipping the lever, the wooden board with the mirror fragments folds suddenly into the light and reflects the sun. All of a sudden the ceiling was a thousand refracted colours; every rainbow, every glittering ray bright like a sunrise above them, all about the hanging rafters of Mydei’s bedroom.

Mydeimos’ face lights up suddenly. It is shocked, for a moment, and a little scared at the sparkles that reflect and scatter so close to his face. Then the fear clears, and what is left behind is only awe. It was no expression Phainon yet seen from such a being; eyes, bright and shining as gems, mouth parted, lips upturned.

Happy. He was happy.

“Is this like daylight?” he asks in wonder.

Phainon nods. “Yes. Except daylight is everywhere, I guess.”

“Everywhere,” Mydei whispers. Absolute desire stains his voice deep blue. “I would like to see that. Light, everywhere. I think it would be beautiful, like this.”

“It is. Oh, it can be so beautiful when we see it through the shadows. Sometimes we all watch it in the village, during the solstice, gathered about the heartfire. And when the sun sets over the river, the colours are far brighter than this. They can be orange and purple and–”

The world stills.

A sharp slice of pain causes Phainon to hiss, drawing his hand close to his chest. Where he fiddled with his contraption, his finger had split on the old mirror shards.

And a single bead of blood shines on his fingertip, red as the sunset.

As though all the light and sound has been sucked from the room, suddenly even the fire feels cold on his back. Phainon can taste it, the infinite hunger, the terrifyingly beautiful desire, the urge to cast himself to his knees and offer his neck to the ancient being sharing the space with him. All Phainon can do to fight it is hold his hand closer to himself, and struggle to meet Mydei's gaze, past the pallid stare that sought to devour him.

“Sorry,” he manages to choke out.

Mydei is frozen. He stares at Phainon’s hand, at the hidden trickle of blood that now tracked down his palm.

“Eat,” the vampire murmurs. All of his body is entirely still.

And Phainon feels terrible, but he shakes his head regardless. “I… I am so sorry, Mydeimos. I… I don't…”

A sadness glitters in Mydei’s eyes, beyond the sharp, visceral, painful hunger that he emanated.

Everything Phainon had done - letting this vampire near him, touch him, watch him eat, feel him swallow - it had been false promises. Phainon knew this. Though this creature intrigued him, he still would not bend to it, this power before him. He could not, for he did not truly want it.

Oh, how terrible Phainon feels in that moment for his teasing, watching the way Mydei’s face falls, the way his jaw sets in understanding and his chest heaves with a sigh. And all the world starts to shimmer as the hunger builds and builds and builds, as Phainon’s throat burns and his lungs singe to ash in his hollow chest. Mydeimos was so terribly hungry, and so desperate to eat, and somehow still restrained himself. At his feet the shadows have condensed. If Phainon looks at the sight with the periphery of his vision, he can almost see them; a dozen hands made of the shadows holding the vampire's feet to the ground.

It is also the first time Phainon feels the danger, really. Mydei had been so unassuming and Phainon so bristled by the concept of being sacrificed to a creature, that until now he had not truly felt it. It bleeds from him like Phainon bleeds too.

This Mydeimos could kill him. This Mydeimos could tear his head from his body in the blink of an eye, and Phainon would not even know he had died.

“You think I do not know you tease me,” the vampire says, quite quietly now.

Phainon’s heart sinks further. “Mydei–”

“You tease me with your neck. With your food. With your blood. You think I am slow to my words, and that I take too long to think,” Mydei says, voice hoarse and empty and hungry and so terribly lonely. “But that is alright, I think. You are not being mean. You are having fun. I know that from your heart now. So thank you for more sun, human Phainon. You should leave, before I lose control.”

And Mydei levels him a stare so bruising, so all-consuming in its pain that Phainon forgets how to breathe at all. It is all inside him, the hunger and the darkness and the pain and the hate, and it never ends and never ends and–

And the vampire sits down, and turns his neck to the ceiling to stare at the false sun while holding his braided hair, and speaks no more words at all.
