He was so hungry. He would never be full. It was all inside him, every moment of the unending starvation, and there was nothing he would not do to fill it, to devour it, to eat and eat and eat–

Waking with a start, it is already midday if the sliver of light and soft heat from the draft are anything to go by. One-hundred-and-thirty-four.

Not even his dreams were safe from the craving to be eaten. Oh, Phainon fears he is already too deep. He fears he has been sent down the river. He fears he was devoured the moment he was strung up against the weeping willow and left for dead.

Enough. Phainon sets about on a sombre mission this time, shaking off all thoughts of an immortal body against his own. He will find what secrets this great cobbled castle holds for good, no matter how much he must comb through the library again and again and again, and leave no dusty scroll or tome or tablet un-turned until he understood all the confusing reasons why both he and Mydei were here.

With his new determination, it does not take long. The library was vast and sprawling and maze-like in its planning, but it was only a library. Phainon trails about the perimeters of each shelf, feeling about the walls or digging through piles of shelved books to see whether some secret was hidden behind them. Come noon, as he is teetering on the creaky ladder as he thumbed through every book on one shelf hoping one might open some contraption, he sees it. Beyond the gap he had forged in the shelf with his searching.

A door. Behind a great bookcase he had yet to circle, and a rather unassuming door it is, for the stone blends in with the embossed wall about it. Phainon swears it had not existed the day before or all the others. Even now it is draped about in shadows so much it almost looked invisible.

“Did you hide this from me?” Phainon asks aloud.

The shadows do not reply. If they did hide the door, Phainon does not know why they chose now to reveal this secret. Still, he goes forwards. The silver knocker is clean though the bronze nails are rusted, and flecks of green slough into his hands as Phainon tries to twist it open. No luck. It was not locked, however, merely stoppered, as though something on the other side had barred it with great weight. He rattles the handle once, twice, then shoves it with all the left side of his shoulder until something gives way. A great tumbling crash follows, scattering books muffled by the rug sending plumes of dust into the dingy, stuffy air that waited on the other side.

A study. The musty scent of dried herbs engulfed him. Long-dead plants sat in rounded jars about the odd shelves, and the walls were crammed to the ceiling with even more books.

And these books were what was missing from Phainon’s knowledge. Just a ghost of a finger over the embossed title of one reveals all; Vampires and Blood Binding; An Experiment of Lifedeath Magick On A Local Specimen Given Willingly.

Magick – the word was bitter, and golden, and new and terribly old. Indeed, in that moment Phainon thinks there must be magick, just as there were shadows that moved and knew life, just as there were creatures older than time itself who fed on human blood to survive. Of all these concepts, magick should be the most normal, to Phainon, but it appears still the strangest of them to believe.

And all of the tomes here spelled only of dark magick, littered about a mahogany desk embossed in red and gold. Every loosened page or bound journal, as Phainon gazed about the room, filled him only with empty, aching horror. What great mage lived here, once?

Had there been magick all those years ago, when the world was still big and free, when it was not devoured by the shadows that kept them safe? Or had magick come from the shadows, as Phainon supposed all terrible things must have? Not many of the books before mentioned magick. The grove had practised math-e-matics and alchemy, potions and the like. Was that magick, too? Or was magick as taboo as the shadows that ate the world in the end?

On the desk of the study sits a long-dried bottle of ink and a feathered quill in bright shades of forest-green and blue. By their side, a bound leather journal was open to a blank page, far bigger than any book Phainon had seen before. Sitting on the creaky chair, Phainon’s hands come to the pages, stained brown as though seeped with splotches of tea and ash. He peels the paper up and over slowly, so he might come to the very first page, ink long faded and smudged by the hand that wrote it.

I write in this book, as the great mage Acacius Lygus Kuwabara Plato, to record what will millennia advanced be called the greatest study of all; the discovery and the harnessing of humanity's ascension into eternal, unbreaking life.

Phainon stares at it, and feels his heart sink so far into the earth below him that all of his chest is hollow and empty.

This was it? This was the answer to all of his questions, here in a journal bigger than any book Phainon had ever seen? Now he has thumbed open the first page it appeared all the shadows in the room had fled, bleeding from his lantern in fear and escaping through the open door.

A vial has come into my possession. A vial of blood, black and thick as tar. A single sip of such concoction is said to prolong the life of a mortal by decades. Indeed, I hardly believed it, but took it anyway some years ago for devotion to my craft.

It appears what the merchant spoke of was true. Ten years since I took my first sip and I have not aged a day. For these years I have agonised over what next to do, how best to harness this miracle for the greater good of all humanity.

They say it is from a creature, older and more ancient than the world or its magick, elusive and rarely seen by any human who lives to speak the tale of it. Perhaps that is why their blood has such magickal properties, for it works to prolong the life of their chosen prey. Such a being might keep a single blood source alive for centuries. Millennia!

I thought to become a vampire immediately, to take on the burden of such ancient power and wield it myself. But alas, it is clear in the sparse writings that magick is not the domain of the creature of shadows. They sit at odds; for magick is to control the shadows, and a vampire may only befriend them.

It appears I shall have to create one myself if I wish to live for eternity. I very much intend to do so.

I shall master all magick, all greatness shall reside within me. I will become the greatest of all mages, and the master of all beings, and keep within my home a creature that is of entirely my own making, and bend it to my will with my talent.

It will fear me as it will fear all humans, who will know of the power it covets in secret, who will know how to use it for all of time immortal.

Something in Phainon shifts. Breaks, irreparably so, by such strange and incomprehensible words as he sits back with a pounding heart. Though he does not quite understand this jargon Acacius Lygus writes, Phainon does not like his manner of speech, nor what he sought to do. It is wrong. Eternal life? Such things were not for humans, such power would surely rot away one's soul into nothing after only a few centuries of living.

Still, as though compelled, Phainon turns the next page, heart all caught and stuttering in his throat, as though the howling wind that clawed through the gaps in his far-away bedchamber window now tore his tongue to shreds in his mouth.

The specimen has been acquired.

It is a young human, about eleven or twelve. No affinity for magick with a particularly strong genetic disposition to physical strength, such as will be required for the transformation. Its parents, some unimportant rulers of a far away warring state, Castrum Kremnos, have searched all the lands for a mage who can give their child what it wants; to become the man it believes it is inside. I donned a foreign disguise and sexed its body somewhat to prove my good intentions so they might allow me to take the child, but I have no desire to complete the transformation. I will inform its parents it passed as a result of the magickal interference. They should not look for it again.

I shall have to keep it here until it reaches maturity, of course. No matter. I have enough of the substance to sustain myself until then.

Through my extensive research, I have learned that to create such a being as a vampire, one must eat the heart of another vampire. A vampire does not need its heart; and so thus every vampire may make one other in their lifetime, if they please it.

I believe the heart of a sacrifice, doused in the remnants of the blood I own and sufficiently charmed, will suffice nicely.

Of how I will find such a sacrifice, I fear little. There is a quaint village by my new residence, shaded by the mountain and nestled in the valley, called Aedes Elysiae by its inhabitants. Little travel passes through it from the kingdom else or otherwise. I quite suppose, should one day a great barrier of shadow appear at the borders of the forest, they would soon believe the world had been eaten, and no man besides myself would be able to break the spell.

Phainon shuts the journal. The thud echoes empty in his ears, and dust swirls in the stagnant air.

He could not think.

In a trance, he stands. He walks from the room. He closes the door, hand hovering on the handle in dread before he turns away.

No. No, surely not.

It was a lie. It was– it was all a lie.

A human-made lie. A man-made boundary. A– a prison, a cage for an entire village, for centuries. Centuries!

And this Acacius Lygus had… made Mydei? Himself? For some sick experiment?

It is too much to think of. Phainon goes in silence to the dining hall early, sitting in his chair, staring at nothing much at all.

Phainon cannot hide what churns away inside his empty shell when the vampire joins him. The creature, the inhuman immortal being before him, had been human? A human child, taken in by a monster under false pretences, and forcibly transformed for what; one man’s immortality? What did this Lygus mean, talking of sexing a body?

It cannot be right. It makes no sense. Even Mydei, far away though he is across the table, appears affected by Phainon’s angry confusion. The shadows propel him forward, the screaming silence condensing into a singular point as he comes to stand before Phainon while the human wipes his face, only half-finished with his meal but no longer hungry at all.

“Human Phainon is upset,” the vampire says. It is not a question.

“... I am tired. That is all.”

Even Phainon’s own ears cannot disguise the clipped manner of his tone. All of his village, trapped. All of them, trapped! For this creature? For a grand experiment that had no end?

Why had the shadows not told him?

Why had Mydei not told him?

“Not tired,” Mydei says, nose now wrinkled in irritation. “I know when humans are tired, now. Shadows make their eyes dark. I can hear your heart, human Phainon. You are upset.”

Phainon says nothing.

“It is Mydeimos’ fault?”

Phainon blinks, and tries to make his voice softer. It is all tangled in him. He cannot think at all. “No. No, it isn’t your fault, Mydei.”

Mydei hovers, there in that space between them, plates in his hand ready to be cleaned and put away. He shifts forward on the balls of his feet; a strangely human gesture of nervousness.

“I am sorry, human Phainon,” he says, and he almost seems a little angry to be apologising, a little withdrawn and far-away. “I am sorry I want to eat you. It is just what I am.”

At that, Phainon looks up properly at the vampire, but he is gone. The shadows have carried him away, and the silence he leaves is bigger than before.

It takes a long time for Phainon to move again, heavy as his limbs are with this knowledge he has learned.

It cannot be true. It should not be true.

Phainon thinks it is true and hates that he thinks it all the same. He thinks that is why the shadows fled the room when he happened on the book. He thinks this is why Mydei is forbidden from eating and why he fears leaving the castle so terribly much.

So though it terrified him, Phainon returns the next day directly to the study, having hardly slept at all and almost forgot to mark his wall with the charcoal – one-hundred-and-thirty-five. He forges ahead, refusing to bow or cower from whatever else might be written by this terrible Acacius Lygus. If it were all a lie – if the shadows were not the end of the world, but a giant cage meant to contain them – then perhaps the book might offer insight into how to destroy it.

Could they be free, his people? Was there truly a whole world out there?

So there he goes into the quiet, cramped study, and draws up the chair close to the mahogany desk, and sets his lantern neatly to the side before taking a deep breath and turning another page.

Simple village people, easily manipulated as I suspected. It only took a few loose conjurings of shadow visions to set them into a panic, and they appeared on my door to beg for protection.

They believe me to be a vampire through my small disguises, simple as they are, and will offer me food to sustain my body as long as I sustain the protection about their village – and the girls they offer me for ‘food’ I will use to bind the creature to my soul, to keep it caged for all of eternity.

Speaking of, the time has finally arrived. It is far less a human now anyway, for I have not let it leave the dungeon since its arrival. It has grown dreadfully pale from the lack of sun, and speaks strangely, stilted, when it must, though the language it speaks to me is not its mother tongue besides. It never lost its fight despite being trapped for a decade and a half now, and still tries all manner of silly attempts to escape. It tried to gnaw off its own ankle some years ago. I almost fainted at the sight of the bone – not for the gruesomeness, but how terribly fascinating this specimen was to observe in such a state.

It is frankly improbable for any one human to have such determination to fight. It makes one wonder what it might have been, had it been allowed to live at all.

At least it no longer cries for its parents. Perhaps it has forgotten them. They are dead, of course, for the fifteen years since I acquired it. Some war I care little for, though I heard it was a crusade to find their son. No matter.

I doused the heart of the village’s first sacrifice, a young woman named Filia, in the remnants of blood from the vial I acquired decades ago. It was a dangerous gamble, but it surely paid off. After years of being fed raw meat to encourage this transition, the human specimen ate the heart quite easily when it was offered.

The transition appeared painful. The screaming was endless, and one must believe it could hardly think for the crackling of its bones, the slow burning of each millimetre of blood in its veins. The charred smell will surely linger for weeks. To watch its body twist and crack and reform around a power so ancient… it was no beauty words might describe, so I shan’t attempt it.

An interesting affect of the transformation is thus: now it is almost twice the size as its malnourished human form, and its beauty – clear to me, even as a child – is tenfold. One could assume such a transformation is meant to attract one's human prey. Interestingly it seems, too, to have maintained my previous sexing; for its chest has developed as a man's, with all the pectoral muscle and widened shoulders expected of such a sex, yet it still has the genitals of the woman it was born of. How novel.

Phainon sits back for a moment. All he feels is sickness. Nausea, deep inside him, that pokes and prods and tears up his insides.

This was wrong. This was terrible. He should not know this. These words, these sickening memories, need to be cast into the shadows with their writer. Atop its devout wrongness, it was also all terribly confusing. This man had stolen a princely child from its parents, and kept it locked away for years? Had done so under the pretence of… Phainon scans the page again, happening on the phrase ‘sexing’ once more.

Phainon supposed, considering he knew of ancient beings who fed from blood and magickal spells this Lygus performed, that somebody born within an unmatching body was not the strangest thing Phainon had encountered. Is that what Mydei was? A woman… who became a man? It did not make much sense to him, but none of the journal did much anyway. What did Mydei look like, then? Was it wrong of him to wonder? Phainon liked to look at him, and Phainon did not much like girls the way he liked looking at Mydei.

So he presses on, all the anger and sickness and dread layered deep inside him. Flicks a few pages through violent depictions of painful experiments on the ‘immortal’s rejuvenating body,’ notes on terrible quantities like the amount of blood siphoned that month or the amount of prickles from a needle it takes to puncture a vampire's skin, until he comes to a full passage across two entire pages of scrawling ink.

I think, perhaps, I should find a way to silence it.

The first few years of screaming was fascinating, but now it irritates me.

When I used the second sacrifice to create the first blood magick bind, I was surprised by how well it took, how neat and handsome the red diamond looked upon its chest. And when I offered up the third sacrifice, pressed her supple neck to its mouth, it could only pant and sob and gnash its teeth, for the burning pain that lanced about the mark and forbid it from biting down.

I should think I shall use the next girl to create a mark that will forbid it from speaking – nay, making a single sound ever again. That would surely assure me many years of peace and quiet again.

Phainon flips backwards through the pages, scanning for wherever this Acacius Lygus had mentioned a binding spell to forbid Mydei from eating, but finds no mention beforehand. Such a spell had clearly seemed so inconsequential that it was of no matter for this man to note.

Still, Phainon presses on.

It is hungry.

It seems, in fact, that it does not wither or starve from hunger; but the hunger is still exponential. How it must feel, the pain it must experience, faced with an endless mirror of emptiness… One can hardly wait for these first thousand years to conclude. Will it still be able to think in the midst of the pain? Will it be mine entirely?

Even now it can do nothing but gasp and claw at its throat, though already some centuries have passed since its transformation. The hunger is not quelled by mortal food or drink; in fact, such organic material appears to make it quite ill, a violent reaction whereby all the shadows in the room for a moment fled in fear. Fascinating.

It is terrified of me, I believe, but truly unable to recall anything of its mortal life. As I expected. It knows not that it was born a woman, nor that its body is any different from another; only that it is creature, and thing, and vampire, and I am human, and mage, and master.

The last binding went well, though the poor girl Saphascia screamed much on her death. The last blood magick mark I conjured was to forbid the thing from speaking, but Saphascia’s death was to prevent it from seeing. I grew tired of its startled, terrified eyes, the horrible certainty with which it bore into my soul, seeking, it seemed, any weakness with which it might counter me.

The next girl I should think I will keep for a decade or two while she is still pretty, and treat her as a wife. It shall help the loneliness that comes from an eternity of research that awaits me – its body is so cold that even when with it I crave the warmth of a true woman instead.

As for the village, the myth of their existence has truly taken root. Hundreds of years of nothing but themselves mean they have little desire to seek anything beyond their sliver of forest. Of course, I must leave sometimes, to attend great deliveries of food to satiate me or my occasional wife. I am lucky they do not probe the edges of the shadows, for should they seek them when I have weakened the anchor for my passing with chalk and blood, I quite think it would all unravel rather quickly.

There is nothing much left in Phainon capable of processing the words he reads. Still he turns the pages, flipping through great yellowed parchment to the next long verse in a sort of fugue-like trance.

The entries grow sparser at least, the handwriting shakier, though still flowery in prose. Phainon flips through perhaps a hundred pages of nothing much at all – occasional notes on the decade, half a dozen writings on each sacrifice. Sometimes the names of the girls were written, sometimes not. None of them, from what Phainon gathered, lived past fifteen years of their taking, and they seem to have been entranced by some loose blood magick so that setting foot from the castle would surely cause their gruesome death.

And throughout it all, though there was little mention of him, Mydei’s story was woven between the remorseless words. Small scrawled mentions of the thing kept in this man’s dungeon, of the being it had made and caged and owned. With a heaviness deep in his chest, weighing down his lungs and guts and choking his throat with nausea, Phainon turns more pages and forges ahead.

On this date, I have henceforth lived for a thousand years.

I do not know if any human before me has lived this long. I am the first of many; eternal, clever enough to bind the undead, powerful enough to keep a village to myself.

It no longer claws at his throat or gasps in hunger or thirst. It does not do anything, so much so I almost feel sorry for it once more, curled upon the dungeon floor, unseeing eyes dead to the world. It recognises no stimuli. Not even when I touch it, or bring another sacrifice for binding. Perhaps the madness has eclipsed all being at all. Perhaps it is not truly conscious. Perhaps it suffers no longer.

I have been fair to it, I think. It knows not of any other existence. If pain is all one knows, hunger all one feels; surely it cannot despair, for there is nothing for it to hope for? How can one imagine an end to suffering, if there was never even a beginning?

Surely it cannot despair.

Surely it cannot think.

Now the writing begins to drag. Each word is longer than the last, as though the hand that writes them knows not where one ends and the other begins.

How does it find a way, still? How does its hunger eat me?

I feel it in the shadows. They have only grown through the years, and now they hurt me. I have not been able to touch my library for what might be decades now, so great and deep is their presence there, and can only squirrel away to this study and lock the door behind me. Each day is the same; an endless torment, a constant seeking for distraction against its permeating power.

No! I must be strong! I shall be the greatest mage of all, the first immortal human!

It fears me! It is mine to keep!

There must be decades between these passages, Phainon thinks, for the ink is never the same, nor is the handwriting, blurred together as though run over by a fingertip, smudged and speckled as though held under the rain.

The village still believes.

I must believe. I do this for knowledge.

I should not fear it. It is mine.

It cannot see. It cannot speak. It cannot know.

It cannot think It is hungry I am hungry I

I should not fear a nothing. I should not. I should not.

It fears me. It must fear me. I hunger. I

Another page crinkles as Phainon turns it.

She found it.

I feel its hunger in my bones. I will never be free of it. Not now she has given it a name. Not now she has given it hope.

The final few pages are a mess. A single sentence slowly morphs its form, written over and over as the ink begins to falter, as the hand trembles with what it writes.

It is hungry. It fears me. It is hungry. It fears me–

Another page.

It hungers.

It hungers.

It hungers.

And another.

I fear I fear I fear I fear I fear I fear

The final page is blank but for three words.

I hunger.

Phainon closes the journal. There is nothing in him, truly, to imagine all he has read at once. Is it truth? Is it like the books in the library; spinning tales of forgotten, forbidden places, made up stories of the human imagination?

No. He knows, somehow, deep in that ache behind his sternum, that the words he has read are real. He can almost picture them, etched onto his eyelids like the stone carvings of his home they use to bless the hunt.

Mydei was human, once. Mydei was a prince just like in the stories, stolen from his home, made into this ancient being against his will. Kept chained and caged for millennia.

The girls had not been to feed a vampire at all. They had been for blood magick. They had been for some sycophantic fantasy of some maddened old mage.

Oh. Oh, how was Phainon to sort this out? How could he ever understand this all at once?

How could he ever put this right?

Phainon blinks.

And suddenly, the journal is not the only thing on the table.

A small book awaits him. There is no dust on its cover, which shines with embossed silver in the shape of a single droplet of blood. As though it has hidden itself, as though it had wrapped itself in the shadows, it shimmers before Phainon’s gaze, heavy and light about the air at once, leeching the colour from the room around it. Phainon does not want to pick it up and desperately yearns for it.

The silence of the study retreats in terror as he takes it in his hands. Lighter than air, he runs the pad of his fingertip over the silver sigil, and then cracks it open.

Magick. Dark, dark magick, much as this mage Acacius Lygus must have performed. Ancient, unnatural magick – magick that should be heaped beneath a vast expanse of dead and cold and unmoving earth. And Phainon knows, as he thumbs to the first page, that this knowledge should not exist. It should be burned, away from human hands. It must be buried as the dead.

Blood Magick of Binding.

The title sits alone on a page, and feels like sickness, and tastes like metal.

All the air in the room seems to freeze as Phainon comes to the first spell, frosted fractals of ice suddenly crackling though his lungs and lying heavy on his tongue. There before him is a terrible inked image of a writhing woman in pain amidst a chalk circle, with dead bodies piled all about her, screaming and clawing at a face removed of her features entirely. The language about the image is no one Phainon knows, strange symbols and words that look too long to mean anything truly.

Another page. Now the image is that of a two headed cow. One of its eyes is cast to the moon and the other to the pool of blood below, whereupon a snake rises up to wrap about its neck and strangle it, though it clearly makes no move to fight.

Another page. Now a man and a woman lie together, but their mouths are gone – replaced, instead, by a third eye they use to kiss, and about their arms burst terrible boils that ooze yellow puss into the blood-soaked ground.

Another page. A broken arm bone splintered in two, a raven who sits within it to nest. Another. An open wound, the infection the colour of the bleeding sky. Another. Another. A dead thing. A flayed wolf. A thousand swarming flies feasting on a corpse. Somehow, Phainon knows the language that scattered the pages, now, though he could not speak it aloud. Somehow, it has been learned to him.

Another. And another. And another and–

And now the room is hot, a million sparks of flame feasting all at once on every breath he takes, and the pages before him seem to glow, and he tastes iron on his tongue and-

Another-

-another-

-and you read and read and a magick greater than all is within your reach if you never know what it's like to die-

“Human Phainon?”

Phainon looks up.

There is nothing different about the room. The temperature is normal. The shelves are complete. The shadows are not alive. In his hand the book is closed, as though he had never opened it at all.

Draped in the darkness of the study, framed by the arched doorway, Mydei seemed to be made of sorrow where he stared at Phainon.

His voice was small. The cooking mittens on his hands slough from them like dead skin, and the flour in his hair sits still. His gaze, forever golden and warm and intense, is now guarded as it flickered between Phainon, the journal, and the book of spells he holds.

“It is all a lie,” Phainon says suddenly. He feels the weight of the world and it is terrible and too much for one man to bear. “All of it. Right? That’s it. It’s all a big, stupid lie. He– he created you, and trapped you here, and experimented on you, and trapped my village too, and– The man, his name was Acacius Lygus. And he was a mage. He held you captive here, didn’t he? Bound you with the girls and, oh, Mydei- there is a whole world out there! The shadows are not real, it is false daemons, it is blood magick. Tell me, is it true? Is this truth?”

Mydei stares at him, looking all of a sudden terribly forlorn.

“I made human dinner,” he says, as though it cannot be stopped.

“Does it look as though I wish to eat? Look at me, Mydeimos! How can I- how can I eat after learning of this?” Phainon explodes, surges to his feet in rage. He is not angry at Mydei in any manner. Rather, he is furious at the world he believed small but was actually big. “He held you captive here, didn’t he? And you did not tell me? That this– all of this is false, that you did not eat the girls, that you did not ask for sacrifices– He did it with this, didn’t he? Forbid you from eating, and speaking, and seeing and everything else, all with this? This blood magick?”

Phainon raises the book.

Mydei hisses in sudden, terrifying pain. All his skin begins to smoke and the room lights up bright as the sun, as though lightning cleaves the castle in two. The red markings etched into Mydei’s body take to glowing, rippling with painful pinpricks of light like stars bursting under his flesh.

And Mydei tears at him, screaming, mouth open and teeth bared–

No. Mydei tears past him, tries to bend the shadows to escape and they do not listen to him, tries to sink to the ground and it will not take him–

–and the vampire is thrown backwards by the force of his terror, books tumbling over his limp body where he slams into a library shelf, a strange hoarse scream echoing in his chest until Phainon shoves the binding book on the table and slams the door to the study. Then and only then does Mydei stop screaming; and he lays gasping and shaking in the silence that he so often brought.

A great look of betrayal coats his handsome face as he looks at Phainon.

And Phainon feels empty, suddenly. Sapped of all his energy, his limbs are heavy and he stumbles against the wall. Why had he shouted? He did not like to shout. It never got anyone anywhere faster to raise one’s voice and demand answers. Especially towards this innocent being, berating him for something he had no control over, something he might not even understand.

The book, Phainon thinks, though knows not why. It had sought to make him angry. It has sought to make him cruel.

“Mydei,” he begins slowly, and tries to approach the vampire, leaning on the shelves to support his weakened legs. “I am sorry- I really am, I did not know, I-”

Mydei is not listening to him. He is curled up as a flower against the shelf he had been thrown against, clutching his neck as he gasped, body rippling with tremors. The world about him warps – and for a moment, Phainon feels the shadows like the warmth of a dozen bodies pressed against him, feels the thin veil of this world and that of magick hum across his skin; and they tell him of a great pain, and great darkness, and a hunger that never ends and a silence that never ends and there is nothing but pain and nothing but pain and nothing but pain and and our Mydeimos will one day see the sun–

“Mydei,” he gasps again, shaking the voices from his mind. “I’m sorry. I swear, it was the book that–”

The rest of his words are stolen from him. Mydei’s face twists suddenly in a great fury and fear, and bears to meet Phainon’s with an inhuman anger. All the silence in the world presses down on Phainon’s chest, tearing his lungs from him, ripping him up from the inside out, boiling his blood and scraping the marrow from his bones.

Teeth bared clean as picked pearls from the riverside clams, Mydei’s hiss is ugly and rabid, face suddenly feral as he rises to his feet with unnatural swiftness. It is not human, his face anymore. It is much like a wolf, a canine with a snout and sharp eyes and gaunt cheeks like a fleshless skeleton.

The shadows come with the raise of the vampire’s hand, and they take Phainon in their grasp, as though physical, as though real. Painful claws dig into his shoulders, and they drag him from the study as his scrambling feet scrape against the wooden splinters of the floor, raking his flesh as Mydei rises from his fall and stalks towards him. Wild blonde hair flies about the vampire, his teeth bared and braid long undone, the tendons in his neck white with fury non-tempered and entirely out of control.

And Mydei is pushing. Pushing Phainon out of the library with the shadows at his command, pushing him down the stone corridor, battering him against the walls as he goes, and it is all Phainon can do to fight the tearing of his clothes with little sway, crying out at the hands that rake him from the shadows, the screaming that blankets his thoughts– and Mydei pushes him and pushes him back into that bedchamber that first caged him. The door slams shut and the lock clicks loudly. All the dust floats in the air, settling eventually, where Phainon is forced into a heap on the floor.

Phainon is alone. He pants, staring at the sliver of space between the door and the stone floor, before collapsing entirely into himself, hands around his neck as though he, too, had not eaten in millennia, bleeding from the claw marks on his shoulders and his back.

Four days.

That is how long Phainon spends locked in his room once again. The first night he does not move at all, exhaustion thread through every inch of his body from facing such dark magick and ancient anger in turn. He knows his back is scratched and torn and warm blood dribbles down his shoulders, and all he does is roll over and stare at the ceiling and try to breathe until the pain dissipates.

The second day he rises. Cleans himself in the sink with still shaking hands, ignores the sight of himself in the old copper mirror he stole from Mydei’s room. By the third day, though the hunger gnaws his stomach hollow, and he shouts and stomps and rattles his bedposts and calls the vampire's name, he still receives nothing in return. Not a sound. Not even a shadow moving at the edges of his vision.

Phainon cannot even read to pass the time; for every time he picks up a book he pictures his hands suddenly a thousand years old, wrinkled and withered with time, blue veins mapping them like bubbling rivers. The same hands as a man who might seek to find the secret to immortality. The same hands doused in the blood of countless young girls. The same hands who kept Mydei captive for over a thousand years.

How unfathomable a time. In all his life, in all of every life – every person in the village who had ever lived or would ever live – Phainon thinks no time would be enough to understand the suffering of those in this castle. Each woman they gave for a sacrifice was under false pretences. They were not used to feed a creature benevolent only when full, who, though ancient and great and terrifying, helped them keep the shadows at bay. Nothing of the sort. They had been giving, for centuries, for millennia, young girls to a mad sorcerer, a mage who bound them to his home, who used them for a brief spark of inspiration or twisted fantasy-wife then slaughtered them to imprison a helpless being.

Phainon almost groans at the thought, curled up on his bed as he held his stomach and picturing Mydei cowering below him, the marks on his skin glowing as the book was held to his face.

So much suffering, for so very long.

Mydei was so terribly hungry, because Mydei had never eaten. Not since he had been human.

And once, Mydeimos had been human.

Another groan wracks Phainon as he sees what he should have the whole time. Mydei, gentle and forceful and confused but always brave. He did not falter when Phainon demanded food from him, and brought the only food he knew from his time in a dungeon; raw meat. He did not falter when Phainon pressed to free himself, to wander the halls of the castle that had imprisoned him, to snoop and pry into such a terrible, haunting place that had held him captive for so long. He did not falter learning to make bread, kneading and pressing and baking a loaf to perfection, or when he let Phainon touch his hair, braid it and stopper it with gold to match his eyes, or when he watched Phainon in the library, reading through the same words as his captor, tracing his path without knowing he walked it.

“Mydei! Mydeimos!”

The fourth day had come if the cool evening draft blustering through the boarded-up window was anything to go by. But Phainon could not handle it anymore, this waiting. It was not in his nature, he decides, to wallow or lament for much longer than three days.

Not only must Phainon put right this hurt of this creature, he must put right the caging of them all.

Eventually, with enough racket made and a few pointed shouts directed at the shadows formed by his oil lamp, he feels it. That ancient presence, swelling and rising all within him, a hunger so great it devours him, a terror so real it shakes him; but the silence does not greet him there before in his room. It is separated in some way by the stone door between the bedchambers and the hallway. Mydei had come, but he would not enter.

Silence. This was a human silence as Phainon crowds against the door, pressing his fingertips into the grooves of the ancient yew wood.

“Mydei, I am sorry,” he says, and desperately tries to convey the depth of his horror. “I did not mean to get angry at you. I was confused by what I had read, and took it out on you, and then the book influenced me. It changed me for a moment. It is not your fault. You have only been kind to me, even though you took me. I am sorry.”

Silence.

“I have no desire to do blood magick, if you are worried about that. I swear it. I can- I will take the book and bury it, or burn it, or whatever you need to feel safe. It is not good. It is not right for such knowledge to exist.”

Silence.

“What is in there- it is evil. Evil. It scares me.” Was Phainon talking about the magick, or the journal? He did not know. Both, he thinks, for they both were equally horrifying. His hands feel stained by them equally, a blood that he is sure would not wash from his skin even if he took to the places the books said, great oceans of water as far as the eye could see, and scrubbed his flesh until he could see bone. “I am sorry I tempted you with my blood. I took advantage of your hunger but I– I didn't know it had been that long. I did not know you had never eaten. I swear it. I was upset that my village might be caged just as you were. I am sorry.”

Silence.

The great absence does not move or change, but Phainon knows it is there. He can hear it, though what he hears is nothing, the inhuman silence of a creature who did not need to breathe to live. All of Phainon’s body longs to touch it, to bend to it, to crave it. To see Mydei, to watch the lantern light flicker in his eyes, to do as he had these past months and go about this great castle knowing the vampire watches him somewhere in the shadows.

The door clicks. It opens slowly, letting Phainon lean back from it and come face to face with the other.

Mydei stands on the other side. He is draped in the shadows. They move about his feet and up the wall, unable to grasp him but clearly trying. Yet he stands, fists clenched and face scared, and stares at Phainon.

“Follow,” he says quietly.

“Where?” Phainon manages, though all the sounds get stuck in his throat.

Mydei rocks on his feet once, then holds out his hand. It is human, the gesture, and though he was so often still as stone – now, he shakes a little, determined in its fear.

“Follow,” he repeats, and this time he is firm.

So Phainon takes his hand.

Such a touch he does not need to think of or consider anymore. That cold hand slips over his own, smooth as silk, firm and strong. Their fingers piece together as though they had been made that way, somewhere in the empty space before existence, and Phainon lets himself be led by this touch, through winding corridors whose cold stone now tells a very different story, whose shadows wept and cried for those it had seen and not saved.

Down, down they go, when they come to a thin circular staircase lit only by a few candles hung from stoppers on the damp wall. Deep into the dungeon, into the basement, each step further into the cold earth, colder until Phainon’s breath fogged in little puffs of white before him, darker until it pressed in on the flame lamp he still carried at his side. Mydei does not falter, but Phainon feels it still – a great sadness, a great pain emanating from him.

Eventually the staircase opens up into a hollowed room. A cave, barely, for its jagged blackstone walls and strange counter-tops carved into the perimeter. It smelt of damp and mould and death.

Here, the sun had never reached at all.

And on the ground before them in this gaping cavern was a semi-circle of chalk patterned with a cleaved gap in the centre. And beyond that; chains attached to a single silver shackle, latched to the wall, split clean down the middle as though by a sword.

Phainon stares at it, this singular silver bolt, and feels it all rise in him, the dread and terror and hunger of a thousand years. This room, he thinks, no man or monster should go. This should be buried. This should be rotten. This was a grave for the living. This was death for the undead.

“Trapped me, with silver,” Mydei whispers. His eyes, glassy and unseeing, gaze upon the silver shackle, and they almost swim with tears, though Phainon does not think a creature such as a vampire can cry.

Then Mydei grasps his thigh, and raises his slacks to expose his ankle.

There, wrapped about his left leg, was what must have been a scar – though it resembled no scar Phainon had seen from those injured hunting in the village, or patterning the knees of children who slipped and fell on their cobblestone paths. This was a deep, pulsing purple. A burn, tearing the skin apart.

It was still burning, Phainon realises with a sickness. It would never stop burning. It was eternal as the thing that it burned.

Mydei drops his hand, and the wound disappears under his slacks.

“Nothing before this,” he says quietly. “All time, only this. Born here, and know no else.”

Phainon remembers what the journal had written, of this creature's past as a human, and it rises in him as the water of the well. “Mydeimos…”

Mydei holds up his hand to stop him. “Listen,” he says, though the word is hard to him. “I… know not what he wrote, the man. Knew not of his name, then, or who he was. But to me, he was all there was. You understand, human Phainon? All there was.” His hand drops again, and he looks to the chalk in a frothing anger. “I was not knowing of what you said, either. He did not tell me that shadow boundary was magick, too. That your village trapped, too. He did not speak much to me, for I could not reply. Only stuck tubes in me, or hurt me in ex-peri-ment. I am sorry he trapped your village. I am sorry he trapped you too.”

Before Phainon can respond, Mydei has stepped over to one of the carved counter-tops, the black surface flickering like obsidian in the light from the stairway. With his movement the fire in Phainon’s oil lamp jumps suddenly across the floor, dancing across the blackstone before settling in a wall-brazier and bathing the dungeon in muted orange. What must be a hundred glass bottles stoppered with silver line shelves and caskets behind the counter-top, all filled with something thick and black and shiny like oil, glittering like water beneath the setting sun.

“This, why he kept me. Vampire blood is immortality for humans. So… he made binds, from death magick. To keep me his. To keep me contained.” Mydeimos’ hands come to his own chest. They probe the red marks around his neck, the flames that lick up where his pulse once would have been. “Do not speak. Do not leave. Do not anger. Do not walk. Do not fight.” Up to his face drag his fingertips and press into the diamond punched beneath his right eye, and a great sadness and terror and fear overcomes Phainon, bleeding from the vampire as his face glazed over. “Do not see,” he chokes out, and drops his hand, as though he does not wish to remember the eternal darkness.

“You can see now,” Phainon says, though whether it is a reassurance or a question, he does not know. His voice echoes strangely in the dungeon room; no living being was meant to be here, and yet he was.

There was so much blood, here. So much of Mydeimos siphoned over decades, clearly for this Acacius Lygus’ sycophantic experiments for immortality.

“Now, I can see, yes,” Mydei agrees. “Most of the binds were broken by death, for he was arrogant. Magick needs-” He pushes his hands together, frowning. “The things. In the library.”

“Bookends?”

“Yes. To keep it falling off. Some have bookends, when he thought of them. Bookends on this one, on my wrist. This one is not to touch any girl. So I could not take the sacrifice before you, the other girl, with hair like pepper. And… and this one. This one has bookends too.” He presses into his chest, pulling apart the soft frills of his white shirt to show the diamond sitting between his breast. “This one is the first, and the truest. Bound in death. Bound beyond it. Clever, this one, and powerful. Do not eat.” Mydei stares at the chalk in disdain. “He needed bookend, here. For one day, he thought, when he had mastered all magick, he would become like me.”

“You cannot eat someone unless they want it... because only he would have wanted it?”

“Yes. Only he would want it. Only he knew me. Only he captured me. One day, he said, I would bite him, and he would eat my heart, and he would be like me. But now he is dead. Silly human. Undying does not die.”

Phainon stares at Mydeimos, and the sigh that leaves his mouth is warm, and wanting, and terribly lonely too.

“You have never eaten,” he says.

Mydei’s gaze flickers. “...No. Never eaten. Not once.”

“But you live?”

“I live. Hunger cannot kill those like me. Only cause madness. Only cause pain.” Then Mydeimos almost smiles, a small, twisted thing, as he holds out his hand and all the shadows in the room rush towards it, dancing on his fingers before settling back into place. “The shadows know my hunger, for I am made of shadows, and they are made of me. So they sought him, when I could not. They made him fear me. In the end, I think he was mad too.”

“Did you… ever fear him?”

“No,” Mydei says, a rising anger in his voice. “Feared his magick, and feared his bind. But never him. For he was human; undying cannot fear any human. Only wait. Only outlive.” Then he falters, and looks down at the floor. “At least, I thought I cannot fear any human. But I feared a little, I think, seeing you in his book room. I thought, what if human Phainon wants to live forever, too? What if he can do magick, too? What if he chains me, and keeps me here also? I do not want human Phainon dead. But I would kill him. Tear out his neck if he used book. He would be dead, then, and he is nice to me. I would be sad, even though he is annoying, and loud, and too much in my spaces.”

A deep breath rattles in the cold silent space. Mydeimos, calming himself with a human gesture he clearly did not need.

“I am glad I am not dead,” Phainon offers.

“Hmph. Of course you are. You are like her.”

“Like.. her?”

“The last girl,” Mydei whispers, and now his voice is warm as a fire, crackling like a hearth. “She was brave, and kind, and clever. She found out his secret. She found me. She would read to me, and promised to help me see the sun.” His soft, barely-there smile falters. “Wanted to promise to help her too. But I could not. She gave me this name, Mydeimos. But she kept her name to herself. She said it was all she had, now. She said it was hers. No one else's."

Mydei stares at the floor, as a spot where the chalk pattern is thin, and a single unlit candle sits half-burned by a book spattered with old, dried blood.

The last girl, Phainon knows. The one who did not cry as they lashed her to the bark. Still she was nameless, even in death.

“He found out. He said he would sacrifice her. Do not hear, would be next bind. So I would be forever in nothingness. But she was clever. She knew she would die for my nothingness. So when time came, she hid broken glass in mouth, and pierced him as he did ritual of binding. This made magick incomplete. It rup-tur-ed. Killed them both. Broke the silver shackle. And then… I… was free.”

Mydei stares at the dash in the chalk, staring at something far away that Phainon would never be able to grasp.

To picture a Mydei so new to the world yet so old, seeing for the first time in a millennia and a half, moving from the only chained patch of stone he knew for a thousand years was almost too much to bear. Coming into an empty, cold castle with two mangled corpses before him, pumping blood onto the floor.

“Still could not eat. Them. When they died,” Mydei mumbles, face all twisted in pain. “Felt the blood. It was warm, with life. But could not eat it. This bind is clever. Even in death, it forbids me.”

Then Mydei turns to Phainon, and a great sadness eats his voice up between them. “And then I took you, human Phainon, like he took them,” he says, voice hollow and so, so lonely. “Maybe, I thought, one day you will like me, and let me eat, because you are nice, and brave like the last girl. I want to eat you lots, but I also want to talk to you, and make you food, and have you brush my hair. It is not your fault you are my food, human Phainon, and tell me no. If I had choice, with him, I would have said no every time.”

Quiet descends. The air is a little lighter, now, though nothing has changed. All the horrors of the past have bled into the wet cave walls. They drip and shine with droplets of fresh water, seeping back into the great belly of the earth they stood within.

Phainon stares at the vials of blood twinkling at them both. How much pain was in them, this thing that Mydei had not been willing to give but had been stolen from him anyway.

Phainon does not think, for he does not need to. He takes two giant strides over to the shelf closest to him, hooks his forearm around a platter containing half a dozen vials of vampire blood, and swipes it onto the floor.

The crash startles the immortal creature, who in a blur of the shadows is against the other wall, staring aghast at the half-shattered glass leaking his blood onto the wet cavern floor. Phainon kicks aside the metal tray and storms to the next shelf, catching now two dozen vials in a big heave and watching them all shatter too.

“Well?” he asks, turning to the vampire who stares at him with some unreadable fascination. “Are you going to help me? You’re a lot stronger than me.”

Tentatively Mydei steps forward, with a strange sort of slowness unlike any human. He reaches out a hand. He stares at the jars before him, on a thin shelf hemmed flat like a fishscale.

He pushes.

The glasses tumble and turn over each other like dominoes, splintering open and oozing his blood down the wall.

And there is a twisting of the vampire’s lips at the sight. It is something almost akin to a smile.

There they go about destroying all the rest. It takes some time, for where the glass shatters and breaks and splinters across the floor Phainon must step carefully so not to cut up his feet or ankles, and there are jars tucked away in corners, or left stoppered behind the counter that must be picked out individually. Still, Phainon knows he will not stop until it is all destroyed, and takes much secret joy watching the determination with which Mydei picks up each individual jar and throws them to the ground with enough force to watch them explode with a sound like the clap of thunder and fizzing sparkles of lightning.

“There,” Phainon says when it is done, hands on his hips, surveying the carnage. The dungeon is unrecognisable, the oil-slick blood seeping into the rivulets of the floor, climbing the walls, all of the place sparkling with the shards of glass that scatter it. “Much better. Don’t you think?”

And Mydei’s stare holds so long on Phainon’s face, so bright and gold it is, that all the dungeon feels flooded now with warmth, and all the deaths the damp walls have seen are memories neither of them can reach. And Phainon does not mind it really, this being captured, when clearly it was the only relationship this vampire Mydeimos understood.

Phainon cannot help his grin, big and wide and happy as he feels despite learning such terrible things.

Somewhere, the world was big. Bigger than this dungeon. Bigger than Aedes Elysiae.

And he would find a way to it, that promised dawn just out of reach. He would lay the path with his own two hands.

And when they go to leave, Phainon takes his foot and smears the chalk not yet seeped in blood all about the floor until it does not look like a cage at all, and Mydei stares at him with that small, twisted smile, and does not look back as he leaves, but walks each step by Phainon’s side, the shadows behind him in time.

With his hands covered by the cooking mittens he borrowed from the kitchen, the next day Phainon goes to Acacius Lygus’ study with new determination. Sitting upon the desk is the small book of blood magick, unassuming and perfectly normal though he holds it gingerly, with only one gloved hand. All throughout Phainon’s hurried journey through the castle it makes no move to turn him or influence him, and by the time Phainon has shoved it into the dungeon and hurried back up the staircase, it is like it never existed at all. He bars the door with an old candelabra and the splintered half of a picture frame, and dusts his sweaty brow with a huff.

Such magick was evil. He would have no part of it. The world would have no part of it; for Phainon would find a way to free their village, and he would use no blood magick to do so.

But the rest of the study offers troves of untold riches. Not all magick was terrible, and ugly, and rotten and putrid. Some was beautiful, Phainon thinks, leafing through the other books of the study that told of magick for happiness, for joy, for love. Clearly this Acacius Lygus has little care for such beautiful magick, arrogant and terrible as he had been. But Phainon does. He grasps these books with care where he cards through them, holding them how Mydeimos held his throat while he ate.

Phainon was quite tired of being told what was and had to be. Their world was small. The shadows were unable to be fought. There was nothing else outside of Aedes Elysiae, and staring at the shimmering horizon of their river was useless, childish fantasy. He was a sacrifice for a terrible creature and would know no peace again.

He had believed it, too. There was nothing for him in this life. He would do as he was meant to, and never act out or speak up, and go about with marrying a woman and grow old enough to be on the council when the next sacrifice needed to be found and decide who would be given in turn.

Not anymore. Not now.

Phainon would find a way to work this magick. He would force it, if needs be. He was nothing if not obstinate. In some strange way he lived with a vampire after all, and had not yet become its food out of sheer stubbornness.

A new dawn rises on a world where Phainon, of all in his village, of all in the world he once believed to be this small; knows the truth. When Phainon goes to bed the next week or so it is with a shining, content gemstone embedded deep into his beating heart. They would hardly believe it, when it happened. When all the shadows disappeared and they were free. None of them even knew they were caged.

Might he be a hero? Might he be like the princes and warriors and knights in the books he read – might everyone love him too?

He had learned a few names, too, from the journal. Filia. Saphascia.

Not the last girl, still. She was nameless on every page, every sliver of memory left of her. Phainon thinks, if she kept her name to herself on purpose, then she would probably be quite proud of the fact that it had worked.

She was the reason Mydei had ever escaped at all. Phainon can remember her much clearer now, standing in the glade tied to the weeping willow. She had not cried then. He wondered if she had cried before the last ritual happened, when she knew she would die for another. He doubts it.

How might he go about honouring them? Perhaps, when he could leave the castle after convincing Mydei in the future, he might set up each of them a grave. They had died for a madman, yes. Been forgotten on purpose. But Phainon would make sure they would be remembered as saviours, at least. Somehow, in some way, he would do this too.

And still he goes about thumbing the letters at night, Phainon reads of Σ’s ecstasy again and again and again, and now all of a sudden pictures this Helektra with wild yellow-red hair and sunset eyes, and a pointed nose and thick plush lips. Imagines that the giving of blood is somehow a version of magick that is good, and that the hunger a vampire felt was really a completion of this goodness, a fulfilment of what is right about the world, what nature has declared equal.

It seemed almost too good to be true. That he might exist in a world where Mydei was not some cunning, evil monstrosity who had taken him to chain him. Rather, Mydei had been the one to suffer. So terribly alone he had suffered, and for so terribly long that it all makes sense; why he would not know what a human ate, why he was so wary of Phainon going about his castle or cleaning his room up or braiding his hair. Why his hunger was so great it seemed almost to eat the air about him, to devour anything he sought to covet with his unending, agonising starvation.

And a smaller part of Phainon wonders, though he shoves it down and about and twists it all up in knots so he hardly thinks of it, what Mydei might look like below his linen shirts and beige slacks. If he was different just as this Acacius Lygus said. Whether Phainon should change what he pictured when Mydei was with him, when he read the letters again and again and again. He did not truly know what was meant by such a concept of the body changing gender. Everything had once seemed so set -- life and death and being and doing, and now it all seemed like the riverbank; what once was firm could be flooded or withdrawn. What appeared a boundary was really a crossroad.

And Phainon keeps living knowing all of these things with a lightness about his body as he goes to the library every day, now with even more wonder as he imagines what it might be should the shadows disappear.

How big was the world truly? How much has he yet to learn?

Could he break the spell? Would he?

Mydei is still wary, at least. Wary of what specifically is hard for Phainon to understand. Perhaps he fears a world where the human he wants to eat knows how great his hunger has become and why. Perhaps he fears a world where Phainon never agrees to let him feed. But he is not a vampire easily scared; more briefly panicked, held back by his restraint. How maddened he must feel with starvation. How much of a wonder it was that he could do anything at all.

Phainon can feel him now. Watching him in the shadows as he curls up in the library with a book on The Origins of Magick Rituals within the Styxian Covens.

“You can join me, you know,” Phainon says to the shadows. Clearly his direct prose makes the vampire panic, for the shadows flicker and fade suddenly, then return with some trepidation.

With a fold and warp of the darkness Mydei is before him. Yet to begin his cooking for the day, he is dressed neatly, with his hair a little messy to one side. It is clear that, after centuries of being forbidden most movement, Mydei found a lot of comfort in not moving. So when he stands there entirely still, and his clever eyes track all of Phainon leafing through a book on magickal barrier rituals and their properties, it does not bother Phainon so much as it makes him curious.

Mydei does not sit down. He does not pick up a book. He stands there, arms by his side, watching Phainon intently.

“Can you read?” Phainon asks the other. He is not sure how much this creature retained from his time in such captivity, after all.

Mydei stares at him, unused to being spoken to while he stalked Phainon about. “I can read,” he says, indignant.

“Then you can join me. Read a book. Maybe you’ll discover something to help us both get out of this cage."

So Mydei does join him there on the floor. Stiffly, back too straight and legs folded uncomfortably, he gingerly picks up the book nearest to him and holds it outstretched on one hand.

He opens it, eyeing the way Phainon held the book with both hands while he read. Shifts about with his shoulders and tries to match the angle that Phainon turned a page.

And Mydei did turn the pages. In time, exactly, with Phainon’s page turning. His eyes do not look at the book at all, but instead watch the human intently.

“You are not reading,” Phainon says pointedly.

Mydei huffs. “Mydeimos is learning to do it right. Like with cooking.”

“This isn’t like cooking. You can read however you feel comfortable. Here– like this.”

And Phainon reaches out and takes Mydei’s hands so easily. Guides them to hold the book with less tension, and comes around even to his back, to smooth out the hardness of his shoulders to trail down his spine and let his hand ease his waist relaxed.

“See?” he says, but all of his tongue feels swollen and heavy, suddenly, for Mydei looks up at him through those pretty eyelashes, and meets his stare so bruising and dangerous and full of hunger Phainon finds he can hardly breathe at all.

“This is… better reading?” Mydei says.

Phainon gulps. He cannot pull away. He is picturing Mydei’s lips on his. Biting him, tearing him apart from the inside out.

Eating him. Devouring him. Leaving him for dead as he bled out into the pages of the book still clutched in his hand.

Mydei grows impatient without an answer. He turns back to his book and begins to read. This he does by taking his finger and pressing it to the page, and there he goes very, very slowly, sounding out each word quietly under his breath. It’s unclear if he’s really understanding the words, or just simply saying them aloud.

And Phainon is watching. Watching the movement of his lips, the pretty way the light of his oil lamp danced on his face. The frills of his white shirt patterning the muscle underneath, the single ringlet of orange hair curled over his forehead.

“Your heart is loud, human Phainon,” Mydei muses as he moves on to the next line.

Phainon jumps backwards. Away. He clears his throat, and forces what he hopes sounds like a nonchalant, teasing laugh. “It's always loud to you. You have hearing like a bat.”

And when Mydei licks upwards against the wound and probes his tongue into the slit punctured by his teeth, Phainon does come, there in his slacks as all his body tenses and the stars print themselves into his skin. The hitched breath is stolen by Mydei’s blood-slicked hand pressing his chin impossibly further upwards, as the other comes to force Phainon’s waist flush against his so the warmth can be chased from his heart. Phainon comes with a wanton moan, with shaking that splinters the world in half, with such a miserable, complete pleasure he fears tears might bead in his eyes as it takes him.

Moaning, writing, lost to his pleasure; Phainon cannot ride out his orgasm, still and eternal as it feels, for his vision is too blurry, his mind too lost. The tongue against his neck sinks back into the wound and his body shudders a final, heaving breath, and all the world closes in on him, and all of his vision goes dark.
