chapters.html:
In his dreams, Phainon meets a girl.

She is tall. Her hair is braided to one side, and she wears a neat chiton with circular golden clasps on both of her shoulders. She does not speak. Rather, she walks just ahead of him, trailing her fingers across the red flowers that bloom in the endless fields they traverse, leaving smears of blood across each petal. And no matter how fast Phainon runs, she gets no closer nor further, though Phainon does not mind this, and understands that what is between them is greater than time. He thinks he recognises her. He does not know from where.

Then he wakes, and it feels as though he has indeed been running through fields for hours. The groan sounds in his chest at the heavy weight atop him, pressing into the bruises he knows must be mottled into his waist and neck, crushing his lungs with them.

When he opens his eyes, however, he finds the weight is not metaphorical. He is wrapped in what must be a dozen blankets and quilts and stitched woollen towels. And atop them all, straddling his chest, was Mydeimos.

“Good… morning?” Phainon manages with a hoarse, crackling voice. His throat burns. His vision splinters and cracks and forms around his throbbing headache.

Mydei’s intense stare bores into him. “You are not dead.”

“Uh, no. I don’t think so.”

Mydei considers this for a moment. Then in a blur he is sitting by the bedside on a chair taken from the dining room.

“...Sorry. Could not stop eating you. Even when you went to sleep, I had few more big sips. Maybe I took too much. You were sleeping one whole day and night and almost day again. I counted, and added tally to the wall you like.”

Phainon groans as he sits up. Placed all over the stone floor were cups of… tea? Seeped lemon water? It was hard to tell. Some were still simmering with steam. His hand comes to his pounding head and there is a bandage wrapped around it, tied with a rudimentary knot that tickles his ear.

“What is this?” he asks, at a loss.

Mydei holds up a book. It was similar to the cooking book in the kitchen, but filled instead with illustrations detailing treatments for every manner of basic ailment and injury.

“If a human is sick, a human gets help. I did not know how to help, but I went in library and asked the shadows to help. Found it in the pictures. Sick humans drink hot drinks, and have lots of blankets, and are wrapped up in the head.”

Despite the pain of his body, Phainon cannot help his smile, the soft laughter that quickly turns into a wince.

“Thank you Mydeimos, for taking care of me,” he says, enjoying how the vampire sets the book down with some sort of self-importance, as though he knew he was correct all along.

The pain of Phainon's throat pulsed in time with the pounding of his head. Yet when his fingers ghost the bites he knew sunk into his muscle, and come away sticky with remnants of scabbing blood, all he feels is a rushing warmth deep in his gut. All he knows is a pull somewhere behind his sternum, dragging him towards the creature at his side, tying them together as though one yarn string wrapped around them both.

It is a connection to more than the vampire, Phainon realises. At the edges of his vision shimmer the world and its shadows, bending towards him with spindly fingertips.

“I can see them.” Phainon lets the focus of his eyes drift away and watches the shadows shift and hum from the corners of the room. “The shadows. They are– they are colourful.”

“Yes. They do not mind you much anymore, now you have fed me. So that is good, and maybe they don’t mind you seeing their colour too.”

“But– they are alive. Actually alive.”

“No. They are undead, like me. They are mirror. They are friend.”

This was too much for Phainon’s pounding head. He winces, massaging his temple again. Still dizzy, every part of his body ached and swayed. “How did I taste?” he asks instead.

Mydei’s eyes flicker. “Like… eternity.”

“You are still hungry?”

A slow, hesitant nod. Phainon supposed the hunger this creature felt was exponential, after all. Phainon bares his neck – yet though Mydei swallows loudly, he does not move to drink.

“I am used to hunger. You, not used to no blood,” he says quite determinedly, despite the lingering desire with which his gaze holds on Phainon’s bruised neck. “So when you are better, I will get more blood. If… if you want to give it me.”

Phainon has to look away for the rush of blinding heat that sears his cheeks thinking of Mydeimos atop him on the dining table, thighs pressed between his, wet tongue at his neck and teeth at his pulse–

“It felt really good for me, too,” he manages, shaking the image from his mind. “You can have my blood again, Mydei. When I am better. Your hunting worked.”

Mydei shines with pride. There he goes about setting up another cup of tea, disappearing in a flurry of shadows and appearing with the boiling pot; of which Phainon lets him, content to have the other seem as though he is helping, though he really did not need three dozen cups of the stuff all placed about the room.

Then the vampire teeters on the balls of his feet again, surveying Phainon wrapped in the blankets with the bandage around his head.

“Lots of blood between your legs,” he says eventually.

Phainon almost spits out what he sips with shaky hands. “Excuse me?”

Mydei blinks at him, then nods towards his slacks. “When feeding from you, all your blood went there. Your human arousal made your blood sweeter like when I give you good food.” Mydei frowns, as though he is truly thinking of it for the first time. “Am I meant to bite there instead?”

“No,” Phainon chokes out. “No biting there, please.”

“... Hmph. Now all your blood is in your face.”

“Yes, thank you for letting me know.”

“You are welcome,” the vampire says, and disappears. He returns soon enough, now holding another hot drink and some recently baked woven bread bites and lentil soup, and Phainon goes to take the platter only to have it snatched back with Mydei demanding he feed Phainon just like the other pictures of sick humans in the book.

Part of Phainon wanted to protest that this was a bit much, but Mydei was so earnest and kind and, if he were honest, had Phainon had been the one eating for the first time in a thousand years, he would probably do everything he could to keep that food around a little longer too.

So he opens his mouth. Mydei dips the bread in the tea as Phainon oft did. Lets him take a hearty bite, and wipe his mouth with a woollen towel after. Phainon has to bite back his smile at the feeling of an immortal, ancient creature harbouring a power older than time feeding him like a babe. When his tongue lingers on the spoon of broth fed into his mouth, swipes around for the dregs of delicious salty herb, he watches with fascination how Mydei’s tongue follows the same pattern in his own mouth. Even now he ate in time with Phainon, gaze lingering on the human’s lips.

“Thank you, Mydei. I feel much better now.”

“No. Thank you, human Phainon.” The vampire is quite serious, and holds up another spoon of broth. “For the first time in my life, I have started a day with less pain than before.”

Mydei leaves him alone for some time after the meal, disappearing into the shadows much like he had those first few weeks Phainon was locked in this room. It is only then that Phainon can sort out his other problem. As he carefully unwinds himself from the blankets and comes to wash his face in the washroom, splashing the spring water against his burning cheeks, he sees how deep and brutal the bruises sunk into his neck are. Yet he does not hate them in any regard. He wears them with pride, in some way, the mottled brown and green and purple, the divots sunk into his muscle where teeth had punctured their mark. He was quite dizzy still, and the constantly pulsing shadows at the corners of his vision did not help.

He had given in. It hadn’t taken much convincing at all, really. Just the knowledge that what he was doing wasn’t supplying some terrible creature with what it believed it was entitled to, but instead giving up a part of himself for a vampire who had suffered for so, terribly long. Perhaps Phainon saw himself a little too much as a saviour. He does not mind. What was so terrible about wanting to save people? About feeling good when he did good?

And then he comes to his slacks. The nice ones he had stolen from the wardrobe trunk in Mydei’s room. With a grimace he unwinds the cord belt and peels them from his body, crusted and dry about the crotch and thighs as they were.

It had been the best orgasm of his life, though the others he could hardly remember, stolen teenage pleasures as they had been.

Phainon shakes his head, scraping clean his slacks in the sink and wincing with each movement. Mydei had worked him to climax on purpose. Had figured out quickly it made his feeding better, and not held back in his abandon of chasing Phainon’s pleasure for him. And Phainon had ground into his leg like he was some dog trying to hump another in his desperation.

A thigh, between his legs. A gasp into cold lips. Teeth at his neck, a tongue pressing to the wound, almost inside him in desperation, eating and eating and satiating that hunger–

Phainon groans. His head throbs, and half-naked in his washroom he finds it a little ridiculous to get aroused again, covered in bruises and pathetic as he looked.

He was here, now. He was a vampire's food. A very handsome, earnest vampire, who seemed not to care that Phainon had reached some sort of sexual completion being fed from. If anything Mydei seemed excited by the prospect, curious and willing to indulge his food for a sweeter taste. What was human arousal in the face of the greatest meal he had ever eaten? The only meal?

As he pulls on some spare slacks, all of his thoughts are filled only with Mydei. Mydei at his neck, Mydei between his legs, Mydei, and Mydei, and–

A snarl sends sudden ice-cold prickles down his neck. He turns quickly, dirty clothes in his hand long forgotten.

And Mydei is in the washroom doorway. In his hand he holds a bronze platter with Phainon’s favourite bread, as well as a soft dip with baked potato and salted, dry brine. His teeth are sharp where they are bared.

The shadows envelop Phainon suddenly and –screaming and screaming and– he is back in bed, under the twenty blankets wrapped tight so he can hardly shift around.

Phainon is quick to protest despite his aching bones. “Mydei, please. I can move around. I just need to take it slow until all my blood comes back.”

Mydei clearly does not want to listen to him as he sits by bedside again. “You are my food. I eat you. But humans are fragile. Humans cannot eat raw meat, or they die. Humans cannot lose too much blood, or they die. Humans cannot leave castle, or they die. I know these things now. You think I am foolish, human Phainon? You cannot die, because then my food dies. I will not be hungry again.”

“One more day,” Phainon offers him. “One more day in bed, then I can get back to the library.”

Mydei stares at him. It is clear the vampire does not want to give in easily, but also does not want to hold Phainon captive so directly; that this is truly an act of care on his part, controlling as it seemed. “Two,” he leverages.

“Alright. Two more days.”

Mydei visibly relaxes. The shadows chatter about him in their shared joy. Phainon watches them from the corner of his eye jump across Mydei’s shoulders, trail around his arm and swirl around his hands as though they laughed with him, as though they knew Phainon as friend now too.



☽


During these two days, Phainon forms a plan.

It is faint. Barely there, for how little he knew or understood of this world he had been thrust into. But it was forming in the interim, shaping around new thoughts and desires and wants.

Phainon wanted. Phainon had never really wanted before.

In the meantime, the two days are not the worst being doted on by the oddly polite vampire he had come to know personally. Mydei has a wonderful knack for only ever needing to learn something once; the moment an action had been demonstrated to him, it was written into him, much like cooking or learning to wash clothes. So the immortal learns very quickly how best to take care of Phainon, how to feed him with one hand and feel him swallow with the other, how to set the lamp low for the human to sleep while Phainon tries not to toss and turn knowing a vampire stared at him, unblinking and silent, all throughout the night.

Still, for the habit Phainon unfolds the letters while Mydei is gone cooking, tracing the words with a smile on his face. It is just as this Σ said. The ecstasy had completed Phainon from the inside out. It had felt inhumanely pleasurable; orgasmic, even, to feel the teeth puncture his skin, to give himself up entirely and be used.

–our legs fit together, mine atop hers. Though she is craven with want for my blood, she is also mine entirely, as she tells me every night before I sleep in her arms. So it is me who commands her, ancient and undying as she is, to grind into my open legs, to devour my singing pleasure with a bite into my wrist–

It had been better than the letters, he thinks. Even more so for how fitted and neat it felt inside him. Indeed, every thing that made him human now felt elevated, rounded, carved out in the shape of a vampire’s bite. He truly was made to feed another. He almost feels bad for those who lashed him to the weeping willow all those months ago; nobody else in the village would ever know such completion as he did. There was no part of his being that was not made to subsist this creature – that is how they had both been made as predator and prey. It gave him purpose. It gave him desire.

Was that what they were, then? Hunter and hunted? Human food and vampire who needed to be fed?

Something in Phainon does not like that thought, but does not know how to sort it out either, and he puts it away purposefully with the letters before Mydei returns.

He had a plan now. He knew what he wanted and he would find a way to get it.

So after the two days of rest Mydei forces him to take Phainon finds himself back in the library with urgency – one-hundred-and-seventy-four. The bruises of his neck were mottled now, sinking into his chest and fizzling into greens and yellows against his freckles. He could not move his head too much too fast lest he got too dizzy, but besides that he thinks his body has been quite resilient to becoming vampire's food and losing so much blood it had pooled below him like the burst banks of a river.

It was in this study he would seek answers about how to destroy the shadow boundary, of course. How to free his village from centuries of being caged.

But mostly, he has decided with some strange selfishness, answers about how to free Mydei entirely.

There was something about it, the intense desire that swept him away, that demanded he find a way to be Mydei’s only thought for the rest of his immortal life. The connection they had sustained now existed beyond just the bite they had shared. Mydei was kind to him. Mydei was irritated by him. Phainon adored both of these feelings, and he also felt inside him the deep, shifting sorrow of Mydei’s past that the vampire refused to talk of in detail.

How he must have suffered, still, and maintained his hope.

Phainon would destroy that which still bound him to that Acacius Lygus. He would take the markings on himself if need be. Through whatever magick was required, Phainon would free the vampire named Mydeimos and become his entirely.

Even if Mydei chose to feed from another after he was truly free. Phainon ignores the lance of ugly jealousy that strikes him at the thought. Mydei could feed from whomever he desired – that is what Phainon wanted to give back to him. Choice in his hunger. Decision in his immortal life.

It is strange, where and when Phainon steps about now as he goes towards the study. Suddenly the pulse of the world thuds in time with his heartbeat. All the threads of the shadows shimmer at the edges of his vision; and the threads were made of shadows, somehow, or the absence of them. It was as though the world was always humming, and while before he had been deaf to such a sound, now it was clear to him. The world was alive much like Mydei was alive. It was undead.

There was much to learn. He is quick to tumble most of the books from Lygus’ shelves to the floor, and goes about sorting them into two big piles: the useful and useless. There was much useless stuff to him that he had skimmed over before. Jargon or complicated histories of magick, books dedicated to the complex angle of ritual salt for a summoning spell specific to a geographical place. Nothing Phainon would have use for, caged as they were in the forest and riverside.

There would have been a ritual to bring forth the shadows, that much is clear. Trawling through Acacius Lygus’ journal reveals little in the manner of what ritual that might have been. For that was what spells were; not shouting out words apropos, or some sort of innate magickal power like Mydei possessed with the shadows. Rather, the ‘affinity’ with magick, as Lygus had written, was some sort of relationship with the world around them all. And this relationship mirrored that between humans – it could be one of control, of coercion, of caging or chaining, or it could be one of love, of joy, of friendship or of pleasure.

So Phainon figures that if he could ask nicely enough like with Mydei and his shadows – and perhaps give a precise offering as these books spelled out, specific plants or dried herbs, spring water or wine or slickened oil – the world might listen to him, and it might dissipate the boundaries of shadow.

And Phainon had befriended a vampire. How difficult might the world be in turn?

The next book he thumbs through as the air grows warm with a late-autumn evening cooped up on the study floor as he was, cross-legged and surrounded by books, is even more interesting to Phainon. There he learns of what those who dabbled in magery called anchors.

The mage had only mentioned them in his journal. Such an understanding of blood magick was clearly rudimentary to him. But there was an anchor for every blood magick spell apparently, and this Acacius Lygus had specialised in such.

The anchor is a conduit, the book details. The gate between worlds. There the shadows may choose to pass through if the spell is complete, and set about completing their side of the bargain, so to speak. This anchor may be physical; a marking of blood, a loss of a limb. It may be metaphysical; a constant feeling, a memory. It may be a shadow itself; a friend, a foe, a chained being or a celebrated lover. So long as the anchor exists, so too does the ritual continue in perpetuo, until something as violent as death or love brings it to its end.

Many of Mydei’s anchors were clearly his markings. Each of them represented the thing that was to control him. Do not eat. Do not see. Do not stand. Do not shout.

Bookends, Phainon realises, thinking of how Mydei had described them. Anchors were bookends. The things that kept the magick complete. And while Acacius Lygus’ death had ruptured many of them, not all of them appeared so easy to break.

So to bring forth the shadows that seemed to eat and eat and eat the world those thousand and five-hundred years ago, this Acacius Lygus would have set out a precise ritual, drawing shapes with chalk at various degrees of north and south, making intricate circles with salt on the floor to ward off bad entities. He would have called upon the world to release the shadows about the village through the conduit of pain, and bound the spell to an item he believed would not be interfered with even upon his death.

What that item might be was the mystery plaguing Phainon. If some of Mydei’s markings were not tied to Lygus’ death but instead to another anchor, he thinks it safe to assume they must be anchored to the same thing. What forbade Mydei from eating was what allowed the shadows to cage Aedes Elysiae.

So to destroy them both, Phainon needed to find this anchor.

All of a sudden, considering all the information he had learned spinning round and around in his head, Phainon suddenly can feel a movement through the shadows. It starts as a tickle at the back of his throat and then ripples down his spine like fingertips tracing the knobbled bone, where it comes to press the point where his lower back dimpled into two.

And Mydei appears at the entrance to the study in a blur of said darkness.

Phainon cannot stop it. The book in his hand cascades to the floor and his body tremors with the sudden urge to present himself, to fall to his knees and bear his neck and fill in this things infinite, beautiful hunger–

“Human dinner-oh.”

The vampire pauses. His hands clench where they hang at his sides, covered in flour from kneading. His nose twitches, and his eyes almost blink into slits as he regards Phainon.

The hunger pours from him thick and fast, much as the first time they met. His teeth are even sharpened where his plush lips hang open in surprise, and Phainon can finally see in the bright firelight the glittering points of his canines, the serrated edges that had so easily sluiced open his neck.

Was the vampire feeling it too? This new connection, this sudden urge to latch to Phainon’s neck and drink and drink and–

Mydei shakes his head. Steps backwards once. “How are you loud in my mind?” he complains, focusing now on Phainon with something akin to irritation. He drops a new shirt on the table with a huff. “You are so annoying, human Phainon. Cannot even be my food quietly. Change into this. Dinner ready.”

Though Phainon has to take a few moments to compose himself and make sure the hardness in his slacks isn’t so obvious, he goes as usual to the dining hall as commanded, a box of miscellaneous items from the study tucked against his hip. He wears the shirt Mydei had dropped off for him of course, and cannot help how lacy it felt all around his chest. It was hardly a tunic, really, half-see-though and made entirely of embroidered roses and shimmering threads of thorns. He felt quite exposed, but Mydei makes a pleased sound in the back of his throat when he enters, and Phainon knows what little blood he had managed to reproduce the last few days was hot in his cheeks like stained wine.

Mydei had set the table very nicely as he always did, with Phainon’s steaming hot dinner on his bronze platter, and Phainon felt a little bad putting the wooden box on the table and beginning to lay out the objects.

“What is that?” Mydei asks, still much displeased at the distraction from ogling Phainon’s naked, bruised chest.

“The books mentioned an anchor. I thought if I brought all the stuff before you that he liked, you might be able to tell if any of them are magickal like your markings while I eat.”

Mydei’s nose wrinkles. “No magick in that box. Put it away. Want to feel my food eat.”

Phainon cannot help his grin at the vampire being so blunt. He does as he is told and sets the box firmly to the side. There they come to sit as they have for so long, Mydei before him, knees slot between his, hand on Phainon’s chin and feeling each swallow and bite with bleeding desire. Now the ache was a little more beautiful. A little less painful, a little more full of yearning. Mydei knows what it is like to eat after so many years. He knows how he can be satiated, and watches with a hungering desire bright red in its shine, picturing the next time he can devour the human in his arms.

Phainon sets down his ladle half way through. He pauses, surveying the Mydei who devoured him.

He tilts his head a little.

Mydei’s gaze flickers. It focuses on Phainon’s pulse, then darts away quickly. “No. You must recover. Or you will fall asleep again and not wake up.”

It is clear the vampire is exerting a lot of restraint. Perhaps it is a bad idea, but Phainon reaches over to the box and fishes out one of the small tins from the study. Opening it reveals a small sewing kit, something Phainon thinks Acacius Lygus would never have owned himself but might have once belonged to a girl he stole from the village many decades ago, for the needles were made out of fish bone and the thread long dry and brittle.

With sure hands Phainon fumbles out the ivory needle, brings it to his finger, and pricks it. Red blood beads in a pretty droplet on his fingertip.

In a flash, Mydei’s chair is gone. The vampire is somehow on his knees, holding Phainon’s arm in absolute awe. His eyes blink, slit sideways until they are nothing but devouring, golden shadows; inhumane, divine, animalistic in their hunger.

“So you can taste it while I finish eating,” Phainon tells him.

Mydei needs no encouragement. A tongue flicks out and licks the wet bead, and this time Phainon has the joy of watching the vampire’s face crumble, shine, break into sweet-singing, ravaging desire. Another lick, and another. The cold mouth envelops Phainon’s finger completely, slick tongue slowly pressing against the pinprick of pain, drawing out the smallest smears of blood with much difficulty. Brow furrowing, Mydei salivates in hunger and awe, shuffling closer on his knees and taking to grasp Phainon’s arm in that iron grip.

Phainon’s breath catches. What a sight it was to behold, the powerful being Mydei was there on his knees before Phainon, suckling his finger so desperately he almost appeared mad.

Phainon forgets about his own food pretty quickly.

Instead his other hand comes to Mydei’s hair. The vampire does not pull away from Phainon’s touch, for he takes to it slowly, gently, carding through those golden curls and parting them from the immortal’s face, setting his braid neatly to the side. Hardly breathing, Mydei’s eyes flit up to Phainon and hold, big and hungry and filled with longing as they were. With great difficulty, he peels his lips from Phainon’s finger, wet lip smudged with blood.

“Is this… alright?” he asks. His lips are stained dark scarlet.

Phainon does not know how he manages to speak at such a sight. “Yes. I— uh, is it helpful, at least? For you to taste me without really feeding?”

Mydei nods, the beautiful look in his eye frantic and wholly undeserving to be given to someone like Phainon, surely.

“Yes, human Phainon,” he says with surety. “You are like a forever, to me.”

And oh, how Phainon tries to turn back to his food. He really, truly tries, gathering the bread in his hand, parcelling out with his thumb and forefinger and dipping it in the jam. But he falters as the tongue licks around his finger entirely, swirling about the digit, the need pooling hot and thick and fast inside him as Mydei’s soft, barely-there moan sings above his chewing.

Phainon takes the dull pin.

Phainon presses it to the tendons of his wrist and pricks a bead of blood there too.

Something dangerous flares in Mydei’s eyes. The vampire casts Phainon’s finger from his mouth and lunges at his wrist, pressing his wettened tongue against the tendon to lap up the droplet of blood, lavishing him in that cold saliva.

Phainon pricks himself again. Right in the crook of his elbow until it stings. With all the power in the world behind his hunger, Mydei lunges further up Phainon’s arm, suckling and lapping and laving at the blood. Driven by instinct, Phainon watches Mydei fall to his temptation and it twists and turns and knots inside him deliciously so.

Phainon liked Mydei without his restraint. Though he was thankful such restraint kept him alive, there was something dangerous and wonderful both about Mydei being allowed to be the creature he had been barred from being for so long.

Phainon hesitates, then pricks his neck.

Mydei does not hesitate. In moments those unyielding hands have Phainon’s jaw in grasp, pushing his head back with the flat of his palm to get closer to the blood. Mydei even allows a moment to pass so the droplet might gather enough momentum to trickle into the dip of Phainon’s collarbone, where his blood-streaked tongue comes again to lap it up, sending shivers down the humans spine.

Eventually, when the small prickle of the needle no longer bleeds, Mydei pulls back with a huff and a sigh both. Gasping, heaving in the chest, it is clear the vampire fights some invisible battle as he tries to focus on Phainon’s face.

“Human Phainon not eating,” he manages to say. His voice is edged. Hemmed with desire and thickened lust.

Phainon does not reply. Instead – oh, how terrible he was, how mean and teasing and selfish – he raises the needle again.

He brings it before his face, and pricks his bottom lip.

Mydei hesitates now. Half straddling Phainon’s lap, cold hands come to grasp either side of Phainon’s jaw. Desperately hungry eyes devour the droplet beading on Phainon’s lip, open as he holds his mouth. Both of them are panting, somehow, though Mydei did not need to breathe and Phainon had done nothing but sit still.

Tentatively, Mydei’s tongue licks up the droplet across Phainon’s lip. He lingers. Swallows loudly with the sweet taste. Then again. Again. Phainon moves not an inch, rooted to the spot with his stomach in knots as as the vampire’s cold tongue teased his lips, ran along them, felt every ridge and plushness with abandon.

The vampire is panting, dishevelled and beautiful in Phainon’s arms. He licks again at the beading droplet and moans that deep, shining rumble, eyes fluttering closed as his confidence grows and latches entirely to Phainon’s lips. Clearly he likes the angle, for now his tongue is in Phainon’s mouth, and suddenly Phainon is moving with him, suddenly they are kissing.

Kissing. This was Phainon’s first kiss. It tastes like his own blood, like the remnants of bread he had chased down, like some deep, bruising desire, the passion so heady and heavy and foggy-minded and completely consuming that he finds he can only breathe by chasing the vampire’s lips with his own.

His tongue reaches out and meets Mydei’s properly. Mydei does not flinch back from this, but pushes further into Phainon’s warm mouth, suckling everything he can from his bottom lip. Sharpened teeth scrape Phainon’s tongue and suddenly a burst of metallic blood fills his mouth.

Mydei jerks backwards. Eyes slit and blow wide, the shadows about him moving and forming and reforming with his overwhelming desire. Something dribbles down Phainon’s chin and trails down his chest.

He was here for a reason. Yes, yes. Phainon looks up and around. Follows the chalk, and realises it does not mark a day at all, but he’d kept writing and writing without thinking of what next to scrawl.

Mydeimos. Mydeimos. Mydeimos.

He smiles, a little. The connection had worked, the life magick that tethered his consciousness to another.

Yes. Yes, he was here for Mydei. He was in the shadows. He had given up his physical body, and was here to take something back.

He turns and leaves the room, ignoring the broken glass on the floor.

No girls led him through the castle this time. He feels a little as though they walk behind him instead, flashing soles and long hair and giggling strung on the cold draft, moonlit voices following his echoing steps and whistling through the creaking stones.

There is something terribly wrong about this place. As he goes each corridor the same as the other, all the warmth is bleached from his body, strung out and wrung dry. He feels colourless, inside. He cannot see the shadows at the edges of his vision for they have sunk into his skin.

It is as though he goes further, somehow. Further into this almost-death. By keeping his mind intact in the shadows he has traded some of his true life. His hands feel colder than the handle of the dungeon door they turn. His legs feel like they are trudging through mud.

Each step he takes down, down, down into the dark stairwell echo is like the crushing of ice underfoot. Each breath he takes fogs before him, obscuring the twisting blackstone walls dripping with moss and mould. The obsidian blade he clutches in his hand, which he might have been holding the whole time though he does not remember it before, cuts into his fingers, leaving a dribbling trail of blood behind him. He pays it no mind.

As the cavern of the dungeon opens up before him, it is not empty anymore.

Somehow he knows it was empty before. Now it is not.

Now, sitting at the very end of the dungeon, huddled with their knees to their chest and matted yellow hair tumbling over their shoulder, is a child.

He is tiny. Starved thin, what remains of his clothes was a tattered half-skirt and untied leather boots. He shivers, curled up so small in such a vast, terrifying place he almost did not exist amidst the emptiness. Beneath him a puddle of dark blood glistened on the wet floor. Stagnant. This little boy never stopped bleeding.

When he looks up at Phainon, his eyes are golden. Rich and deep and infinitely terrified.

“Hello, mister,” he says. “Are you here to take me home?”

Phainon could fall to his knees. Though the silence does not end he longs for it to. Longs somehow to cast himself from this waking dream and find himself still tied to the weeping willow all those months ago.

It was Mydeimos’ voice. Young, not yet broken. High-pitched and proud, though clearly he suffered still.

Phainon takes a deep breath, and hurries around the dungeon, sweeping his hands beneath the obsidian counter-tops, checking each unlit torch and shelf. When he finds no key, he returns back to the young Mydeimos with dread, for a shackle is latched to the child's ankle. It leads into the gaping darkness behind him. He comes to crouch before the other, stepping over the line of salt with ease.

“Hello,” he says as bravely as he can, “I am Phainon. I am looking for a girl.”

The boy wrinkles his nose. “I am not a girl, mister,”

“No. No, you definitely are not. What is your name?” he asks, though of course he knows it. The boy does not flinch as Phainon brings his black blade to the chain, to attempt to work loose a rung with the tension around the soldered edge.

“I don’t know,” says the boy. “He took it. He took it away, in my head. I can’t remember it anymore. I want it back. I think it helps me fight him, my name. And he does not like when I fight him. But I won’t ever stop fighting him.”

No, Phainon thinks, biting his lip as he desperately tries to lever the shackle’s bolt apart. Mydeimos never stopped fighting.

“How about Mydeimos? That is a strong name for a strong man.”

“I am not actually a man yet, mister. I will be soon. He promised to make me one if I promised to wait.” Bloody fingernails latch onto Phainon’s hand as Phainon’s blade slips and almost slices his finger off. “Don’t worry about me, mister. You have to find the girl. Like you said.”

Phainon presses the knife into the edge of the silver shackle once again. The metal hisses and burns his skin and he ignores it. Cyrene would not lead him here purposelessly. If she were not with him, that was by her design. What he seeks must be here in plain sight, like Cerydra’s name.

“She’ll come to me,” he says, though hardly believes it. “She is brave. I’ll find her.”

“I don’t know where you’ll find her, mister. I’m the only one here, I swear."

Phainon pauses. His hands shake, and still, and tremble again.

He looks up.

Into the eyes of the memory of Mydeimos, his time as a human given true shape in the shadows. The little boy with his sunken cheeks and big round eyes.

Golden eyes. Golden eyes with that streak of red by the pupil, that spike Phainon had always called a sunset.

“How long have you been here?” he asks the child, and dreads the answer with every part of himself.

The boy meets his stare bravely. “Since the beginning, mister. Since the shadows ate the world and ate me too.”

Oh. All the air leaves Phainon in a slow, despairing sigh.

The anchor wasn’t Cyrene.

It was Mydeimos.

Human Mydeimos, left in the shadows for over a thousand years.

Lygus had mentioned that Mydei had lost all his memories of being a human – as had been expected – but not that he had taken them with some part of the blood magick.

Oh, no part of Mydei had ever been for himself; not his body or his memories or his choices. It had all been taken from him, used and trapped and kept for fruitless fantasy.

The shackle in Phainon’s hands trembles and scalds him. The walls begin to pulse, to spit out dust and droplets of water, the high-ceiling shaking and groaning and threatening collapse.

How was he meant to harm this child? This was not like Cyrene, where he thought he might convince the other to give up the spell and reclaim it. This child knew not what a spell was. He did not even know his own name.

Phainon stares at the blade in his hand. Did he need to do it? Drive forward the black edge, force it into this child's beating heart until he is lifeless and cold?

He could not do that. Sacrificing himself was one thing. Sacrificing another; it would make him no better than Lygus, playing with blood magick, harming those in pursuit of his futile dream.

“You should use my sword, mister. To slice the shackle in two.”

And suddenly the child is holding a sword, though he hadn’t been before. It is a sharp, flat thing, and the blade looks like silver glinting in the darkness, though the head is carved like a lion with a fiery mane.

Phainon wastes no time. Raising the blade and driving the sharp edge down, the moment the silver met silver the shackle it splintered in two with sparks that char the air.

“Come on,” he says to the boy, grasping his hand tightly as the dungeon begins to scream and shudder. “Let’s go home, Mydei.”

The young Mydeimos stares at him, eyes flickering, face streaked with grime. His ankle is rubbed raw and swollen. “My home is far away from here, mister.”

“Well then. We better run really fast.”

As the dungeon begins to crumble, the walls spitting out big chunks of rock that rain down on them and plummet into the oncoming darkness, they do run. Hurtling up the stairs step by step, feet slipping on the black blood that dribbles from every hole in the wall. Behind him Phainon hears only screaming, and in front of him only laughter, and both are so loud as they run and they run that he thinks all he hears is silence in the end.

As they burst into the hallway, he sees her at the end of the corridor. Her form shifts and silts though her kind face is clear.

Cyrene.

Phainon follows her, clutching the little Mydei along. The boy's hand is so small and holds so tightly his fingertips turn white, though he runs with his bruised ankle and blood-soaked thighs like he was born for it. Each pattering step of their feet in time shakes the crumbling castle. Phainon knows where he goes; he follows the girl who in turn follows the light, distant at first but growing and growing, a pinprick then a goblet then a blinding sunrise.

And they burst through the light into a grand hallway. The walls hang fluttering with banners, the face of a goat with horns curled around a star. The place is warm and bright and filled with laughter. At the table, a dozen girls sit and dine and giggle and sing. One plays the lyre. Another dances in circles with her bare feet. They all clap in time to her song.

At the other end of the dining hall Mydeimos is crouched over Phainon’s body somewhere in the real waking world. Stained clothes back over his body, cradling Phainon’s head and stroking his face and murmuring “human Phainon, human Phainon,” as though his voice might bring him back no matter how far he goes.

It is quite strange for Phainon to see himself not breathing. To look down at his own body and be entirely disconnected from it. When he holds out his hand, the one not clutching the child, he sees it pulse and quiver in time with the shadows.

Mydeimos looks up. His eyes dart over Phainon and come to the child who has let go of his hand.

And the young Mydei looks real. Physical, in the world. Somehow Phainon had traded his own body for another, given himself up in place of the child.

At first, the vampire Mydeimos is still. Both of them stare at each other ten paces apart. Mydeimos looks at himself and his eyes are wide, his mouth parted, his hands that pet Phainon entirely still.

Then he moves. Presses a gentle kiss to Phainon’s forehead, and steps over the edges of the ritual runes. Comes to stand before the younger him with something akin to fear.

“Phainon sent you,” he says. It is not a question.

The child’s lip wobbles. He does not look around the place, does not take in being real after so long of being hidden. Instead, he wipes quickly at his eyes, and stares at the vampire before him with awe.

“It worked,” he says, and his voice breaks into a sob and he collapses onto the ground. “It worked. You are a man like he promised. You look like how I feel inside.”

Mydeimos stares at the crying child. His hands twitch, his brow furrows. Clearly he does not know what to do.

“You are the anchor?” he asks.

The child cries and cries and cries human tears, fattening at the corners of his eyes and dripping down his dirty cheeks “I miss the sun. I want to see it, once. Do we see it? Does waiting work?”

The vampire Mydeimos rocks on his heels. Comes to kneel before the child, holds out his hand then pulls it away.

“Yes,” he says after some hesitation. “You see the sun all the time, eventually. And it is beautiful, the sun, and he has a name. His name is Phainon. He is my sun.”

The boys sniffles. Wipes his face just as the vampire Mydeimos did, smearing his tears all around his cheeks. “Phainon. That is the mister who freed me, I think. He said I would get to go home, here.”

Mydei stares, and he stares, and he stares. His gaze is deep and unreadable and aching and warm. It is the sun as it is the shadows. He puts away the knife, the obsidian blade he had used to carve the mark into Phainon’s chest, and holds out his arms.

“Come home, then,” he says. “I am your home.”

The boy is quick to cast himself into Mydeimos’ arms. The moment they touch, the entire world shakes with the force of it. All of Mydei’s markings light up so brilliantly red it is as though the sunset breaks through the clouds, blanketing the room in a pretty blood-red. There the child cries and cries and cries, and clutches the vampire’s shirt and shoulders and arms, and his voice is layered with a thousand years of hunger, and his tears fall like sparkling gems.

The shadows are unstable. Phainon can only stand and stare as the line between the worlds was blurring. Collapsing in on itself. The screaming builds alone in his ears. His body lies dead a few feet from his shimmering, almost smoke-like form.

He was fading. He can feel it in himself. The road he should take back to his body is weakening, the blood of the ritual drying. Soon, he would not exist at all. But he could not return while the child still existed, clutched in Mydeimos’ arms, for he had traded his place to allow the other to be. He could only watch and he knows he is smiling wide.

Besides him, a girl stands.

“You were not the anchor,” Phainon says, watching the boy in Mydei’s arms begin to splinter, to crack as though porcelain.

“No, human Phainon,” Cyrene replies. Her voice is only herself, that night. “I was a bridge.”

All the hallway shudders and groans, the spiralling stone arches above them crying dust that does not land on Phainon’s shadowed body but dusts his corpse those five paces away.

“Can I bring you back, too?” Phainon asks her.

The shadow by his side shakes her head. Her eyes are forest-green.

“I am not alive. I am a memory made of a lovely promise, not the real Cyrene. Her desires live within me and I treasure them, for how strong and brave she was.”

“You care for him more than any other vampire.”

“He is a true friend of the shadows. Our dearest friend. Is it not you who said love was like the shadows? What, then, is love to a shadow itself, except the promise that if one turns around, one can see the sun?”

The castle was collapsing. The stones beneath their feet rising and falling, undulating like a great wave. In Mydei's arms the child is beginning to fracture, to turn faint and fade away. All Phainon can hear is the giggling and the screaming and the silence and the hunger, a hunger that never ends and a darkness that never ends and a pain that never ends–

“Did it hurt her? Dying?”

At that, Cyrene smiles. Her eyes glitter. She is beautiful like a river which reflects the moon.

“No, human Phainon,” she says. “For the shadows held her as she went. She fell asleep in our arms, and she knew she was loved.”

Then Cyrene turns away from the sight of the vampire and his human self becoming one. She walks back to the table surrounded by those dozen girls who feast and laugh and hold their cups up high, and bless him with their many voices. Thank you, human Phainon, they say. You have given him the sun!

“You should run now,” Cyrene tells him, and sits down at the head of the table where a plate of seeded bread and orange juice waits for her. The youngest girl, no more than ten and three, hurries to her side to braid her hair with plucked daisy flowers and ribbon. “Or you will not make it back.”

It is not far to run, though suddenly it feels like a hundred miles are before him. Ten paces between his body and his shadowed self.

Yet each takes an eternity. Each is like he is frozen in time and pushes through the oil-slick air to place one foot on the ground before lifting the other. The child Mydei holds has almost disappeared. His shadow is barely seen, only a few glimmering flecks of darkness in the bright-light room and the faint sound of crying and joy. He is going to die this way, a ghost left between the shadows and the world. He will become like Cyrene. He will never awaken.

And then, he sits up.

He gasps. He is naked amidst the pentagram and chalk. Hair a mess, blood streaked down his chest. The world is not collapsing. The castle still stands. In his body it feels strange, like there is a pane of cold glass between himself and his movements, though as he twitches his hands and wiggles his toes the feeling begins to return.

Shaking hands come to his chest. There, marked in a circle around his shoulders where the knife had carved his blood offering now sat a single glimmering golden line. It was raised slightly against his skin like a scar.

The shadows, he thinks with delightful laughter. They were inside him, now. The spell had been broken, transferred to his own body. He had become the anchor and it had taken no violence or words. He simply gave up his body for a while so the memories of Mydeimos could find their way home.

That is what this line is, he thinks. Mydei’s way home.

And now they were free.

“Phainon!” Mydei calls from where he had finally looked up from his empty arms. In a blink he is beside his human, cradling him again, fussing him. The tears on his cheeks shimmer red and they are full of joy.

Phainon looks up into his eyes, and smiles so big and bright he might be the sun itself. There was no sunset in Mydeimos’ eyes anymore. He was whole again.

He still had his markings, of course. But as Phainon watches, in the low light of the hallway with all the torches put out, they do not glow like they used to, but sit dark and dead and useless.

“You were stupid, still,” the vampire complains, but though he cries his smile is finally wide. “You almost died again. I could feel you weakening. I thought I would lose everything again.”

Phainon cannot help his grin, the kiss he tries to press to Mydei’s lips but finds he is too weak to sit up on his own, the world spinning and jolting as he tries.

“But now you have everything,” he contends when he finally manages to be upright.

“Yes, Phainon,” the vampire says solemnly. “I am whole again. I held myself, and he came home.”

The world shudders and groans. From outside the castle suddenly comes the crashing cacophony of a thousand shards of glass splintering on the floor. It crackles and spurs and sounds like the end of the world comes with thunder.

Though Phainon had never left the castle since he had been taken, somehow he knew the way to go. With much help he staggers to his feet. Throws on his slacks with weak hands, laughing the whole time as Mydei latches his cord belt for him. As they leave the hall his stumbling feet smudge the chalk and salt. He does not even look back.

The door is big, made of old oak and great bronze bolts that have rusted green sown the wood. It opened without a key. Before them stretches the forested hillside topped with the reaching fingers of trees stripped bare for the winter and the harsh breeze scented like wild-berries and river rushes past them both. Mydei must think he only wants to see the sky from inside the castle, for the moment Phainon lurches himself over the stone threshold he is hurtled backwards by shadows at his feet.

“Wait. You cannot leave castle! You will be hurt!”

Phainon laughs. Grasps the vampire holding him back, snaking his hands around his waist tightly to keep himself upright. His body is still weak and he could not care less. “The bindings are all broken, Mydei. All of them. Every one.”

“...All of them?”

“Yours, too. You can eat who you like now, and touch whomever you please.”

Phainon had realised some time ago that Mydei feared him leaving the castle for he believed there was some sort of spell that would hurt him if he did, much like Lygus had charmed upon the girls so they were forced to live and die in these stone walls. But now they were all broken, he could give Mydei the peace of mind that his skin wouldn’t peel off if he felt the fresh air just for a little while.

After a long silence, Mydei says only one lonely, aching sentence. “But I only want to eat you.”

Phainon laughs. It is a gentle sound. There he takes Mydei’s hands, unfurls them from their tense fists. Guides him outside where they can stand free in the darkness of the night.

The sky was broken. Fractured by a thousand golden lines as though glass thrown to the dungeon floor. Bits of it begin to fall, cascading over them like glowing flower petals. And Phainon laughs and laughs and holds out his hands and spins beneath it though he is still weak in his knees and head both. There he sees for the first time the sky without the shadows blurring all the wide world, and they are sharp, and bright, and beautiful. The air is fresh and wind no longer stagnant, cold and sharp with wintertime that stretches into a world far bigger than theirs.

They are free. It had worked. The glittering golden line on Phainon’s torso was proof; he had saved all he loved. He had become a hero.

And he did not care. All he wanted was in his arms, for when he grasps Mydei’s waist and gathers the other into a kiss, the world and its shadows disappear. The lips against his are tender and hungry, and nibble his lip until sweet blood bursts between them and it tastes like freedom and the shadows. Around them the golden petals fall, shimmering and sinking into the ground with the remnants of their magick fading.

And they go dancing around in a circle together while Phainon sings the everlasting song, laughing the whole while, and the world keeps on turning, and all of it is in the palm of their hands.

In the morning, they go to the village.

Or Phainon does. Mydei does not, for the sun would burn him and he fears for the people too.

“Best if you go alone,” he had said. “They will listen to you. Not like me, still, though not their fault.”

So Phainon comes first to his old house in his nice clothes, pointedly chosen for being free of any blood stains and high on his neck to hide his bite-marked bruises. The hut he grew up in is made of cobbled stone and ivy climbs the crumbling walls. The roof is thatched hay, and in their small garden plot the first frost of winter glitters and crunches underfoot.

His mother is already awake when he comes before her. She stares at him across the doorstep, bucket in hand to go to the well, leaning on her cane.

She steps forward. Blue eyes search his own, studying his face for answers she might never understand; why is the sun clear in the sky? Why is the wind brighter, filled with many more things than their river and hillside and village?

Why was her son here alive and not chained in some damp dungeon feeding some almighty being?

She takes his face in her wrinkled hands and presses a kiss to his forehead. Then slow hands slip around his shoulders and take him in a hug.

It is the most she has touched him in years. There he cries. Cries like the shadowy form of Mydei as a child, big retching sobs that wrack his body and pierce the gentle air. Somehow he is on the ground, and she is holding him, and she might be saying sorry but might be saying nothing at all. It does not matter.

He did not do this for her. Not for approval, not for love. That he had given up. And this show of affection does not make up for these things taken from him when his father had passed.

But it is something. It is all he wanted, really, as a child. One long, loving hug.

“Mother, I–”

“Shh,” she says. Her voice is old and cracked with grief. “You are alive. You are not taken from me like he was. I do not care to know anything else.”

And he cries harder, then. So hard his nose runs like he is a babe and stains her old dress dark blue, so hard his throat shrivels up like when he was a nine and suddenly death felt real and pressing and permanent.

So though he came to the village to tell them his story, after his tears have stopped falling he decides he did not need to. Instead, from the hillside where he grew up, he watches. Watches all the people gather in the village square by the crumbling marble pillars waving their hands or huddling their children close to their skirts. The shadows have been broken, the hunters who tracked the border at dawn return to say. Nothing haunts them now. The world outside extends, though how far they cannot tell, and for what means too they come up empty.

Phainon does not go down to tell them. He does not feel the need to, anymore. Once he might have revelled in the chance to return as their hero. Now he thinks he will live how Mydei lives; and be free inside himself too. The village was no longer caged. He had done his duty, and needn’t help them explore a world big to them that once had been small.

Still, when he treks his way back to the castle after his mother bids him farewell with one shaky kiss, he does not expect the knock at the door to sound. He had only just returned, shook the big fur coat he had from his body of all the frost clinging to its fluffy edges, and been taken in by a kiss by Mydei and a laugh and a pressing of their foreheads together. Here he was home, not down in the village. In this vampire’s arms.

But the door suddenly shakes with three quick raps of the silver ring hanging on the other side. Phainon opens the heavy thing expecting a village elder come to shake their pitchforks at him and demand he take them to the creature who had broken their vow and stolen the shadows.

Instead, he faces a woman he does not know.

Behind her are a half-dozen of what Phainon thinks must be the knights written about in all the stories sitting atop great chestnut-dappled stallions. They wear strange white clothing like the books said, and linen skirts and breastplates made of bronze. Their helmets shine with seashell and their horses have feathers in their hair.

“Are you the hero of Aedes Elysiae?” the woman asks.

Phainon looks at her. “I am Phainon. Are you from Okhema?”

The woman is surprised he might know that name. She tells him they are part of Okheman’s scouting contingent. That some twenty years ago the ruler of Okhema had finally set about trying to find a way into the strange shadows that haunted the edges of their borders, for an old book had been found detailing a residence there, a village of a hundred people built by the river they worried was still contained in the magick gone awry. She spoke strangely, with an accent like their languages had diverged in the past thousand years, but many of their words were shared.

“–so we went to the village when we came across the broken shadows, bright as they looked for many miles, and have given them all our supplies and sent for more. Yet most of the village people know not what has happened. They speak of strange creatures and stranger sacrifices. A woman came to us and said to find her son, the hero of Elysiae, here in this crumbling castle. He had found a way through the shadows, she said. He can tell you what occurred.”

Phainon shrugs. The gathering of people is very strange to him, and he wishes he could pick through their clothes and ask questions about where every fastening or coin came from. “There were shadows. I broke them with a spell. That's all, really.”

The knight is absolutely bewildered. “‘That's all?’ Do you even know what you dealt with was magick? Such a boundary we have been unable to pierce for some thousand years, if the ancient texts are to believed. A mage as powerful as yourself should have an audience with the Council of Okhema themselves post haste. They will be quite desperate to know how all of this came about.”

Phainon tries not to laugh. “I am no mage.”

“But– your connection with this magick is something unheard of to us. Come, let us feed you, clothe you properly. You can tell us the story on the way to the city.”

“I am just a friend of the shadows,” he says with a smile. “You should probably go now. My partner is hungry. I can feel him teething on my finger where my hand holds open this door. Is there anything else you need from me before I go?”

And the woman looks at him with such bewilderment, such sudden fear and awe, that Phainon truly does laugh then, and shuts the door with a gentle click. There was no doubt that he wanted to travel the world – go about everywhere he had read in all the stories he poured over with fascination. But he wanted to do so without any sort of attention. To see the world on his own terms; his choice to live, just as Mydei’s, just as the shadows.

“Partner?” the vampire asks with such intensity his eyes look to glow like he hunts. Somehow they are on the floor in the hallway, having made it hardly any distance at all before Mydei had pounced on him to lick and nip at his throat.

Phainon grins, though is certainly bright red after his faux-confident stunt in front of the knights. “If you want, we can be partners. I read it in the books. It means we are, you know. Courting.”

“Hmph. Yes. Of course want,” Mydei declares, and crawls atop him properly to latch to his shoulder. Phainon strokes his head and arches his back into the piercing touch, singing his pleasure the whole time.

In the basement, they burn the books.

The journal and the blood magick book, that is.

Phainon isn’t sure it will work considering what dark magick one of the tomes holds. Yet parchment is only parchment, he supposes, and the world that once was small has now bled away into much bigger. Both Lygus’ words and his actions disappear into smoke. They will never be known again.

“How does it feel? Being whole?” Phainon asks the vampire later. They are curled up in their shared bed, Phainon reading the book on Cifera’s travelling adventures aloud and Mydei listening as he traces all the lines in Phainon’s palm like he memorises them.

“Strange,” the vampire says. “First I thought I could not feel it. Difference between bound and free. Now I can. It feels like breathing did as human. Phainon reaches up and plucks a rogue curl from Mydei’s hair where it has fallen over his forehead. The vampire is quick to disappear and reappear by his side holding the comb, and Phainon smiles as he shifts upright to gather all Mydei’s hair on one shoulder and braid it neatly as he always did. The vampire sighs into the feeling, twisted smile on his lips.

“Tomorrow I am going to do one more magick ritual, but I will need you there. Is that alright?”

The vampire nods, clutching his braid, running his fingers over each bend as he always did. “I trust only you, human Phainon.”

Dawn break is when the spell must be done so he goes in the morning before the winter sun has risen to set up the spell. Phainon had already memorised it. The whole action was theoretical, laid out clumsily in one of the many experimental journals Lygus had kept written by other mages. But somehow he knows that this will work. Maybe it is just as the knights had said; maybe he was not too bad at this magick stuff after all.

Amidst the drawn chalk runes and salt pentagram Phainon stands in front of Mydei. Sips the potion he had made of seeped tea and stinging nettles that tastes like fire where it settles in his chest, and wipes their foreheads both with ash and moonwater. It is an easy ritual. One that takes no time at all, that requires only the ruins and the chalk and the salt be placed a certain way, with no giving of life or pleasure this time.

It is easy, for he knows the shadows will give him this. It is everything they have ever wanted. It is everything they are made for.

“Bite me,” he murmurs to the vampire after he has taken him in a hug.

Mydei does. Sinks his teeth so tenderly into his neck that it almost feels like falling asleep. And as Mydei takes his first gentle sip, Phainon speaks.

“Nam sol umbras facit,”

For the sun makes the shadows.

“Umbrae lucem videant.”

Let the shadows see the light.

A burning pain lights him up inside. Bright as the sun, terrible and scorching, a thousand blades scrape his skin into shreds. He does not cry out. The ecstasy of the feed equates the agony of the blood bind; so for a moment, Phainon almost does not exist at all, caught between the extremes of every existence.

And also for that moment, he hears them. The shadows themselves as always. The chattering, giggling laughter of all those that ferry this spell to completion with ease. Cyrene, and Saphascia, and Filia and all the rest whose names he will never know; they are free now too.

When it is over, Mydei licks him gently. His cold saliva dips into the wounds of his teeth, then he pulls back in shock when he feels what Phainon did. The etched march on the edge of his neck surrounding the bite that had eaten from him.

“A sun?” Mydei asks, cold fingers comforting against the new binding of magick against Phainon's skin.

Phainon takes Mydei's hand. He guides the vampire through the castle at the pace only a human can go. The other lets him. When they come to the heavy wooden door that once confined them both, Mydei trusts the other so much that the vampire does not even notice when Phainon steps outside while still clutching Mydei’s hand.

And the vampire’s arm sits before them, bathed in sunlight.

It does not burn. It does not spit, or smoke, or wither.

The silence is greater than the first night they met. It buzzes in the air, the wonder with which Mydei looks at himself in the sunlight. With how the dawn rose without the shadows; it is brighter even than Phainon ever wondered, and drapes his brown skin in a soft glow.

With trepidation, Mydei steps out into the sunlight entirely. It envelops him. The frills of his shirt shimmer translucent in the brightness, his bare feet sinking into the dewy grass of early-spring.

For a long time Mydei stands there. His face is turned into the sun and his eyes are closed, soaking it up with every part of him that can feel.

“It will not protect you forever each time,” Phainon tells him eventually, when the other has spent many minutes saying nothing at all. “Perhaps an hour, maybe too. Then the shadows will return to the surface and you might start to feel some pain before you burn.”

Mydei is not listening. He smiles so wide and beautiful and unlike any smile he has given before, and he glistens in it, he shines. No sun would compare, Phainon thinks, to the sight of Mydeimos happy.

“It is beautiful,” he murmurs, looking around at the world in its brightness. “You were right, Phainon. The light is everywhere.”

It is in this sunlight that Mydei clearly makes a decision. Sets his shoulders wider like the Prince he once was. He brings his sharp teeth to his wrist, and tears open a small gash against his marble-smooth. That sparkling black blood dribbles down his forearm in rivers. Beneath the sun it is slick with greens and blues, holographic colours that spin and dance much like oil.

And then he holds his wrist out to Phainon.

“My food, forever,” he says.

There is no real decision made – Phainon had already made all his choices. So now it is his turn to bring his lips to Mydei’s bleeding skin, to lap at the blood and suck it with his clumsy human lips. On his tongue Mydei tastes sweet and savoury, like every dinner ever cooked for him, like every ounce of desire and hunger and darkness and light that made both of them complete.

Like poppy-seed bread, he thinks with a grin as he licks the wound clean. Like rye loaf. His favourite.
𖤓


They wait until springtime has truly dawned to set off.

The village is half empty. Many have fled to Okhema to see the city, to seek what trades they needed for a village that had sustained itself with crumbling buildings and paddy-pastures for a thousand years. Most of them were simply trying to escape a place they had not realised caged them, and they speak little of their past to others; the sacrifices of Aedes Elysiae are something to be kept in the past. It is no matter, though, for the village is quickly filled with all manner of visitors instead. Phainon does not go down to meet them, though often they come up to the castle to try to ask him questions or convince him to visit their various homes and fix their lives with magick too. Some try to convince him the creature he might still live with is controlling his mind. Some want to know if the vampire – elusive apparently in every part of the world – is real at all.

He tells them the same he told the Okhemans. He is no mage. He is simply a friend of the shadows, and they should probably go back to the village, or the magickal boundary he had on his castle would strike them with lightning in only a few more minutes.

They always hurry away. They will write of him, he is sure. The elusive hero; the saviour mage who might live with a vampire, who might have charmed the undead. They will make little mention of Mydei other than the rumoured sacrifices he knows the village people spin tall tales of, but Mydei tells him every time he asks that he does not want these strangers to know him or the girls that had been taken; they deserve rest, to be thought of only kindly and not slung around like gossip. And Mydei himself wanted to control who knew his name or could know his story after it had been stolen from him too. This Phainon respects, and quite enjoys messing with the outsiders with his vague answers besides.

But by the time they come to leave their home, it feels strange. This was everything Phainon had ever wanted and never thought he would get. Now he was here on the doorstep to the castle he called home, having spent weeks setting everything just right so that their return in a year would not greet him with only crumbling stone or rotting food.

Standing beside him, as always, was Mydeimos. The vampire carried a backpack of various hearty foods he had cooked for his human, a few spare vials of blood in case he was hungry on their travels, and a pouch of all the gold they found around the castle they could use to trade for the ‘money’ the big cities used as their currency. He wears a great cloak Phainon had stitched together with all the slacks they had torn in half in the heat of the moment when they had been feeding. When the hood is drawn it will cover the vampire's face and body so he would not burn if the spell to keep him in the sun ever weakened.

And that cloak was needed, of course, because they were going to leave the forest. They were going to go far, far away.

They were going to take Mydei home.

On the doorstep to the world, Mydei takes his hand firmly. He does not falter. Still his hands are cold, and they stroke circles against Phainon’s easily.

“I love you like the shadows, human Phainon,” he says.

Phainon looks at the other in shock. This Mydei loved him? Truly loved him?

Well. Well, yes, he supposes then with a grin. If this wasn’t love, then what was? Cerydra and Helektra had loved each other as vampire and human. It was the purest form of love he decides; only this love could sustain another’s life entirely.

“And I love you like the sun, vampire Mydeimos,” Phainon replies with that easy smile.

“Love me like the sun?”

“The sun casts a shadow, and a shadow is proof of the sun. So they exist because of each other, like our love.”

As Mydei rocks on his heels in happiness and his reserved smile twists his lips handsomely, Phainon pulls out from his cord belt a map. It would not be easy, their travel. Mydeimos had less connection with the shadows away from the castle, and they would have to resort to human transportation a lot, a feat difficult when Mydeimos was as beautiful and inhuman as he was. But they could only try, he supposed, as they always had. It would be another adventure. It would be the start of their forever.

And the map is huge. It will take them only to Okhema’s ports, where they hope to board some vessel or buy their own, and set off across the great ‘ocean’ that was wide enough to sail upon.

And they would travel for months and months, and they would go to Castrum Kremnos.

“You are ready?” Phainon asks as he has many times these past few weeks.

Mydei looks into the mundane forest stretching before him, the tips of the trees green with budding leaves, and repeats what he has been practising.

“My name is Mydeimos. Once, I was Prince of Castrum Kremnos. Then, I was captured vampire. Now, I am free, and all myself. And I am ready to go home with my partner Phainon, who is also my forever food that I like to eat, and who is also the one I love like the shadows.”

“You added that last part since last time,” Phainon laughs.

Mydei huffs as he always did, though he is trying to hide his smile. “Of course. Because it is true. Must you be loud during my moment too?”

And they take each other’s hands again, and step out into the sun.
